releases.headline: The audit trail recorded a partial result as a success and scrubbed the fields that say what happened
releases.summary: `warning` was mapped to `success`, so a row describing a partial result read exactly like one with nothing wrong in it, and an outcome the vocabulary did not recognize became `success` too. Separately, the always-redacted field list matched short entries as substrings: `auth` scrubbed `authenticated`, `authservId` and `author`, and `ssn` scrubbed `className`. Both defects removed information from the trail an operator reads after something has gone wrong.

items.title: The WebSocket same-origin default compares the whole origin
items.body:
`b.websocket.isOriginAllowed`'s default compared the `Origin` header's host against the `Host` header. RFC 6454 defines an origin as the triple of scheme, host and port, and neither of those two values carries a scheme, so the check tested one member of three: a page at `http://` the same host passed it. The docstring above it stated that this default closes the cross-site WebSocket hijacking class, and against a network attacker or a mixed-content page at the cleartext origin it did not.

All three members are compared now. The scheme comes from the connection, and the host from the authority the request named, so an HTTP/2 upgrade — which carries no `Host` header at all and was previously refused outright — is compared correctly.

The scheme is resolved the way every other scheme decision in the framework is: from `X-Forwarded-Proto` when the immediate peer satisfies a `trustProxy` predicate, then from the connection, and only for a request that carries no connection to ask from the HTTP/2 `:scheme` pseudo-header. Unlike `:authority`, `:scheme` is a value the client writes, and over cleartext h2c a direct client can send `:scheme: https` on an unencrypted socket; where a socket exists, its encryption state is the half the peer cannot assert. `b.requestHelpers.requestProtocol` reads `:scheme` for every caller, which is what an RFC 8441 extended CONNECT needs — its request is built from headers alone and carries no socket to ask. A deployment terminating TLS at a proxy passes that predicate to `b.websocket.handleUpgrade`, which hands it to the check; without it the backend socket is cleartext and an `https` Origin is a cross-scheme request. `isOriginAllowed` takes the same options as a third argument for callers using it directly.

items.title: The origin check reads the authority an HTTP/2 request named
items.body:
Node does not map the HTTP/2 `:authority` into `req.headers.host`, and this framework's TLS listeners advertise `h2` first, so every current browser negotiates HTTP/2 against them and that header is absent. Five places read it alone and reached two opposite failures from the one premise.

`b.middleware.csrfProtect` built its same-origin baseline by concatenating the scheme with that header, so over HTTP/2 the baseline was a bare scheme, every browser `Origin` mismatched, and the gate **refused every form submission**. The same request with the same token returns 302 over HTTP/1.1 and 403 over HTTP/2. `b.middleware.hostAllowlist` read the absence as a malformed request and denied it as `missing-host`. `b.middleware.cors` inferred no origin at all, `b.middleware.botGuard` stopped recognizing loopback as a secure context, and the 0-RTT replay key hashed an empty component for every HTTP/2 request.

`b.requestHelpers.requestHost` now answers with the `:authority` when one is present and the `Host` otherwise, and the five readers go through it.

It prefers the pseudo-header rather than falling back to it, which closes a second problem: `Host` and `Origin` are both caller text, so a non-browser client over HTTP/2 could write both halves of the comparison and have the check agree with it. `:authority` comes from the connection. Not browser-reachable, since `Host` is a forbidden header name, so this was defense-in-depth rather than a live CSRF path.

A trusted `X-Forwarded-Host` still takes precedence over both, and is still ignored from an untrusted peer.

items.title: An unrecognized audit outcome is no longer recorded as a success
items.body:
`b.audit.safeEmit` normalizes the outcome it is given, and anything the vocabulary did not carry became `success`. A caller that wrote `faliure`, or passed a value from a newer vocabulary than the table knew, recorded a successful operation. On a trail that exists to be read after something went wrong, that is the wrong direction to fail in.

`b.audit.record` refuses an unrecognized outcome, as it did before. `safeEmit` cannot: it is drop-silent by contract, and throwing would lose the row it was called to preserve. It now records `failure` instead, so a typo becomes a row somebody investigates rather than one nobody reads.

An OMITTED outcome is unchanged and still records `success`. Leaving the field off is not a misclassification, it is no classification, and several events already emitted that way; turning them into failures would fill the trail with rows describing things that never went wrong.

The normalizer's targets are also held to the vocabulary when the module loads, so the two lists cannot drift into disagreeing: an entry pointing at a value `record` refuses would silently drop every row that used it.

items.title: A refusal reaches the peer before the connection is torn down
items.body:
All five mail listeners ended the connection and destroyed the socket on the next line. `end()` queues the FIN behind whatever is still in the write buffer, and the `destroy()` did not wait for it, so whether a refusal arrived depended on whether it happened to fit in the kernel socket buffer, which depends on how much the peer sent rather than on anything the server decided.

Measured against an MX with a 1 MiB ceiling and an undeclared `DATA` body: 2 KiB over the limit delivered `552 5.3.4`, 64 KiB over delivered it and then a clean FIN, and 256 KiB over delivered nothing at all and reset the connection. The failure ran the wrong way round. A small overshoot, where retrying is cheap, got the permanent answer; a large one, where retrying is expensive for both ends, got the reset. RFC 5321 section 4.2.1 makes that difference load-bearing: a peer that receives a permanent code stops and reports to its sender, and one that receives nothing has no verdict and re-sends for the whole of its queue lifetime. Several refusals on this path are ones a hostile peer can trigger deliberately, so the reply most worth delivering was the one most likely to be lost.

The socket is now destroyed once the reply has flushed, with the socket's own close and a five-second timer as backstops so a peer that stops reading cannot hold the connection. The session is still marked closed immediately, so a queued command is never executed after a refusal. A connection held open to flush stays counted by `connectionCount()` until it actually closes.

items.title: A JMAP blob download does not take its type from the requester
items.body:
`b.mail.server.jmap`'s download endpoint set `Content-Disposition: attachment` only when a filename was present and matched a narrow pattern. A blob with no filename, or one carrying a space, was served with no disposition at all — which renders inline.

That is what made the response type dangerous. The endpoint takes its type from the download URL's `{type}` variable when the backend reports none, so a response could carry attacker-influenced bytes under a type the URL chose, rendered inline, from an endpoint that requires an authenticated actor. For a mail attachment, whose bytes arrive from outside, `?accept=text/html` was script execution in the application's origin.

Every download is an attachment now, whatever its type, so the bytes are downloaded rather than rendered. An unquotable filename costs the name, not the disposition.

The type itself still follows RFC 8620 section 6.2, which defines that variable as "the type for the server to set in the Content-Type header of the response", since "the blobId only represents the binary data and does not have a content-type innately associated with it". A backend that reports a type wins; otherwise the URL's is used. Neither is written into the header unless it is a well-formed media type, so a type carrying CRLF — raw or folded around a parameter separator — takes the generic type instead of reaching the header or failing the response.

Reachable only through a consumer that implements `mailStore.downloadBlob`, which the framework does not ship — such a consumer inherited the behavior with no warning that it had.

items.title: A CSRF origin refusal names its reason
items.body:
`b.middleware.csrfProtect` refuses a request that carries neither `Origin` nor `Referer` when `requireOrigin` is set. That refusal was audited as `origin/referer: [object Object]`, because the check returned an object on that one path where its four other exits return a reason string and the caller builds the line by concatenation.

The gate itself was never weakened: the object is truthy and the caller compares against null, so the request was refused either way. What was lost is the reason, on the one configuration an operator turns on deliberately, and in the trail it was indistinguishable from any other object that might arrive there later.

items.title: An API key's scope is bound to the credential it belongs to
A sender-policy refusal reaches the client instead of the socket the connection opened on
items.body:
When a composed `senderPolicy` raises, `b.mail.server.submission` refuses the sender, which is the documented fail-closed behavior. The refusal was written to the connection's original socket. The listener requires STARTTLS before it accepts an envelope, so by the time a `MAIL FROM` reaches a sender policy the connection has always been upgraded and that socket is the wrong one: the reply reached nobody and the client waited out the idle timeout.

From the sender's side that is indistinguishable from a dead server, and it is the worst shape a refusal can take, because a client that receives no code cannot classify the failure and re-sends the same message. The refusal now goes to the socket the session is actually on.

An `eslint` rule refuses the shape across all five mail listeners: a handler takes the live socket as a parameter, and a nested function reading the connection's own binding is reported. It asks the scope analyzer which binding a reference resolves to rather than matching the name, so a callback registered on that socket, and a parameter carrying whichever socket is current, are unaffected.

items.title: A DMARC aggregate report is bounded by expansion as well as by size
items.body:
`b.mail.dmarc.parseAggregateReport` capped decompressed size and said nothing about how little input produced it, and the input arrives from anyone who sends a report to a published `rua=` address. It now runs through `b.safeDecompress`, which bounds compressed size, decompressed size and expansion ratio, and records a refusal to the audit trail.

The ratio is set from measurement rather than from the sibling parser's 50:1 default, which would refuse ordinary mail: a generated report reaches 38:1 at 100 records, 63:1 at 1,000 and 109:1 at 10,000, and a report from a single sending host reaches 225:1. The cap sits at 300:1, about three times the largest measured legitimate ratio and about a third of what the gzip format itself can produce. The absolute size cap remains the bound that does the work.

A ZIP-delivered report is named as one instead of failing later as malformed XML. RFC 7489 §7.2.1.1 allows it, and `b.archive.read.zip` reads the entry out; the refusal says so.

Separately, a report of any real size was being refused. The XML parse was given a byte cap and left at the parser's 10,000-element default, and one `<record>` expands to seventeen elements, so a report was refused at about 580 records while the documented record cap is 10,000 — and refused as malformed XML, which names no limit. The element cap is now derived from the record cap.

items.title: The always-redacted field list no longer scrubs by substring on short names
items.body:
Field names are matched case-insensitively and by substring, which is what makes `userPassword` redact under `password`. Six entries are too short for that to mean anything: measured against the field names this framework emits, `auth` matched 93 of them, `sid` 32, `pin` 29, and `ssn` matched `className`.

What was scrubbed is what an operator reads to find out what happened: `authenticated` and `authenticatedAs`, whether a check passed and as whom; `authservId`, the RFC 8601 identifier naming which server wrote an `Authentication-Results` header; `author`, which RFC 5322 section 3.6.2 uses for the `From` party; and, through `sid` and `pin`, `residency`, `sidecar`, `residentKey`, `stepIndex` and `mapping`.

`auth`, `pin`, `sid`, `ssn`, `cvc` and `cvv` are matched as a whole segment of the field name, and as an occurrence at a name boundary so a caller that normalizes its keys to lowercase is covered too: `authcode`, `ssnnumber`, `last4ssn` and `customercvv` are all still redacted, as are the camel forms. Every longer entry keeps substring matching.

What may follow each short name and still be an ordinary word is a closed list, decided from the field names this framework actually emits rather than from the nouns that would make one a secret: enumerating the nouns is open-ended and fails silently on the one nobody listed. `authentication` is readable and `authenticationCode` is a credential, and the two are identical up to the noun, so the exemption is anchored at both ends — a compound that is not on the list is redacted rather than exposed.

items.title: `warning` is an audit outcome
items.body:
It was accepted as a word and mapped to `success`, which is the one thing it cannot mean: `success` and `warning` are the two answers a partial result needs to tell apart. An ingest that stored 490 of 500 records is neither a success nor a denial, and recorded as a success its row is indistinguishable from one that had nothing wrong with it, so the query an operator would run to find partial results returns nothing.

The vocabulary is now `success`, `warning`, `failure`, `denied`, accepted by `b.audit.record` and by `safeEmit`. Advisory and deadline-miss outcomes the framework already emitted — a residency-gate advisory, an incident stage recorded past its deadline — record as `warning` rather than as successes.

Upgrade note: a consumer that queries for `outcome = 'success'` to mean "nothing to look at" now sees fewer rows, which is the point. Rows that previously said `success` because their outcome was unrecognized now say `failure`.

items.title: A message stores every octet the peer sent, whichever way it arrived
items.body:
The `DATA` path stored a message two octets shorter than it was transmitted, because it read the whole `<CRLF>.<CRLF>` terminator as framing. RFC 5321 §4.1.1.4 says the first of those CRLFs "is actually the terminator of the previous line", so it belongs to the mail data, and this framework's own `BDAT` and IMAP `APPEND` paths kept it: two of the four ways a message enters disagreed with the other two.

What that costs is not only two octets. `POP3 RETR` restores a trailing CRLF only when the body lacks one, so a message whose last line is blank still ended with CRLF after the subtraction and the blank line was gone: the account holder received a message one line shorter than the one sent, and a MIME epilogue is made of blank lines. A message with no body lost its header separator entirely, so the stored form contains no `\r\n\r\n` and a DKIM signature over it cannot be evaluated. A consumer storing bodies under a digest got two different blobs for one message depending on which door it came through.

`b.safeSmtp.findDotTerminator` now returns what its own documentation always described, the index where the mail data ends. That index is two octets further on than before, so a caller slicing to it stores what the peer sent. Empty mail data terminates as well: a client answering the 354 with `.\r\n` sends three octets, the CRLF that opens the terminator having ended the `DATA` command line, and the five-byte scan never matched it — the collector waited for a terminator that had already arrived.

`b.safeSmtp.dotStuff` documented a trailing CRLF it does not append. It stuffs and nothing else, and the caller owns the line the terminator needs; the documentation says that now. Both current callers already did it.

DKIM body hashes are unaffected: RFC 6376 §3.4.3 and §3.4.4 each append a CRLF when the body lacks one.

items.title: `GETSCRIPT` closes the literal it announced
items.body:
`b.mail.server.managesieve`'s `GETSCRIPT` announces an octet count, writes the script, and then wrote the CRLF that closes the literal only when the script did not already end with one. A Sieve script ending in CRLF is the ordinary case, so a conforming client read the announced octets and found `OK "GETSCRIPT completed"` where the terminator belongs. RFC 5804 §2.9 puts the CRLF there unconditionally, and the count was already in hand on the line above, so the framing never needed to be inferred from the payload.

A detector refuses the shape: a CRLF written to a socket under a test on what the payload ends with. `b.mail.server.pop3`'s `RETR` is unaffected — it announces no count, so the terminator's leading CRLF has to come from the body or from the server, and it tests the trailing bytes directly.

items.title: A delivery report quotes the headers that were sent
items.body:
`b.mail.send.deliver`'s DSN builder extracted the original header block by decoding the message as UTF-8 first. That decode substitutes U+FFFD for any sequence it cannot read rather than reporting it, and a message off the wire is not guaranteed to be valid UTF-8: a legacy 8-bit header, or a raw byte in an unencoded parameter, survives transmission and did not survive this. The bounce then quoted headers the sender never wrote, which is the part of a delivery report a person reads most closely.

The header block is now located in the message's own bytes. A block that is valid UTF-8 is quoted as before, and the part names the charset, which `text/*` otherwise defaults to US-ASCII. A block that is not valid UTF-8 is carried under `Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64` (RFC 2045 §6.8), so every original octet reaches the reader and the part's label describes the bytes that are actually there.

The block's end was also wrong for one of the two message forms. The separator's own line terminator is two octets when the message uses CRLF and one when it uses bare LF, and a fixed two was added either way, so the same message spelled two ways produced header blocks that differed by more than their line endings. The width is now carried out of the match.

items.title: A DKIM key record with upper-case tag names no longer verifies here
items.body:
RFC 6376 §3.2 interprets tag names case-sensitively. `b.mail.dkim` folded them, so a selector record published as `V=DKIM1; K=rsa; P=<key>` verified here and is refused by every conforming verifier, which finds no `p=` tag and therefore has no public key.

The direction of that is what makes it worth changing: the operator is told their DKIM is correct while the receivers they actually send to treat their mail as unsigned, and nothing on the sending side can see it, because the only party that reports the truth is the receiver. An application checking its own published record against its own key got the lenient answer too.

ARC is the same production by normative import (RFC 8617 §3.8) and had the same behavior; a seal written `I=1` was read as instance 1.

DMARC, BIMI, MTA-STS and TLS-RPT are unchanged. None of those specifications states a case rule for tag names, and reading them strictly would refuse a record and yield no policy at all, which is the wrong direction to fail in.

items.title: `app.listen` rejects on a bind failure instead of ending the process
items.body:
`b.createApp(...).listen()` wrapped its bind in a `try`/`catch`, which sees only a synchronous throw. A bind failure arrives asynchronously as an `error` event on the server, and nothing listened for it, so `EADDRINUSE` and `EACCES` ended the process instead of rejecting the returned promise. The port already being taken is the ordinary way an operator meets this, and what they got was a dead process rather than an error they could report.

The returned promise now rejects with the bind error, matching what the framework's mail listeners and `b.testing.listenOnRandomPort` already do. The handler is removed once the bind succeeds, so a later server error is not swallowed.

items.title: A second `MAIL` inside an open transaction says what is wrong
items.body:
`b.mail.server.submission` and `.mx` refused a second `MAIL FROM` with `503 5.5.1 EHLO/HELO first`. The client had already issued EHLO, successfully, so a reader who trusts the reply goes looking for a session that lost it. RFC 5321 section 4.1.4 describes this case as a sender already specified, and that is what the reply now says.

The verdict was always right, so nothing on the wire is newly accepted or refused. The guard that produced it also tested a session stage neither listener ever assigns, so half of its condition could not exclude anything; it now tests whether a sender is set, which is the condition the specification names.

items.title: `Document-Policy` is not sent by default
items.body:
The default named `document-write`, `unsized-media` and `oversized-images`. The last two came out of the Document Policy origin trial and are not in shipping Chrome, `document-write` is not implemented as a document policy either, and Firefox and Safari do not implement `Document-Policy` at all. The header therefore carried no mitigation and logged one `Unrecognized document policy feature name` warning per feature on every navigation, which is how a real warning gets missed later.

The comment beside it claimed the `document-write` feature disabled the legacy DOM-injection API. It did not. What does is the `require-trusted-types-for 'script'` already in the default Content-Security-Policy: under it that sink is guarded and throws.

`documentPolicy` remains available for an operator targeting a browser that gains support, and `documentPolicyReportOnly` is unchanged. An operator relying on the previous default was relying on nothing; anyone who wants the header back passes it explicitly.

items.title: A build-time dependency of the fuzzing harness is refreshed
items.body: `browserslist` moves from 4.28.4 to 4.28.8 in the fuzz harness lockfile, clearing GHSA-73wf-gq98-2v4g and GHSA-c83g-rgw3-j3cx. It is a transitive development dependency, is not part of the published package, and the framework's runtime dependencies remain empty.

releases.headline: Four mail listeners dispatched a pipelined command against the state as it stood before the previous one finished
releases.summary:
A POP3 client that wrote `USER a`, `PASS a`, `USER b`, `PASS b` in one segment authenticated twice. The guards that refuse a second login read the session stage, and the stage moves only after the credential check resolves, while the reader dispatched every complete line it held without waiting for any of them. All four lines were answered against the state as it stood before the first check finished.

The reader now takes one command, waits for it, and then takes the next. Four listeners shared the shape and all four are fixed; the SMTP listener already worked this way. Alongside it: a retention floor that measured age from a date the sender chose, a STARTTLS upgrade that verified an address-literal peer against `localhost`, and every listener silently accepting option names it does not have.

items.title: A pipelined second credential pair no longer authenticates
items.body:
`b.mail.server.pop3` refuses a second `USER`/`PASS` pair on a session that is already authenticating. It did not: the AUTHORIZATION-state guards read the session stage and the actor, and `PASS` sets both only after the credential check resolves. The reader dispatched every complete line in its buffer without waiting, so a client that wrote both pairs in a single segment had all four answered while the stage was still AUTHORIZATION and the actor still empty. Both pairs were verified concurrently and both entered TRANSACTION.

The reader now takes one command, waits for it to finish, then takes the next. `b.mail.server.imap` and `b.mail.server.managesieve` read the same way and are changed with it; `b.mail.server.mx` already chained its input and is unchanged. Any guard that reads state a later handler writes was unsound in all three, not only the credential pair.

`b.mail.server.submission` holds the client's pipelined remainder on a pending-command flag instead, and already did so for the sender-policy hook. It did not for `AUTH`, so two credential exchanges written in one segment were verified at the same time on a session that was not authenticated yet. The flag is now held there too, set before the verify begins and released on every path.

Waiting for a handler only works if the handler hands its work back, and most did not: they started their work and returned nothing, so the reader had nothing to wait for and took the next command immediately. Every command handler in the three listeners now returns what it starts. The nesting is the part worth naming: POP3's `PASS` did return its credential check, but the session leaves AUTHORIZATION inside a further step that opens the mailbox, so waiting for the check alone still read the next command against a session that was not authenticated yet. That step is returned too, and so is the result of the shared SASL round.

One consequence is visible on the wire: a command that arrives while the previous one is still running is read after it finishes, not during. It is still answered, and a second login is still refused; the refusal now names the state the session actually reached.

Because commands wait, a connection holds more than one at a time, and the limits follow. The line cap applies to a line, checked where a line is taken, so a client that pipelines several short commands is no longer answered `BAD Line too long` for their combined size. What a line cap cannot bound is how many lines are held: `b.mail.server.imap`, `.pop3` and `.managesieve` each accept eight lines' worth of pipelined commands and close the connection past that, so a peer cannot hold a slow handler open and keep sending.

A handler that rejects is answered once, by the listener that already owned that reply, and the connection closes on an error the reader itself raises.

items.title: A retention floor measures arrival, not a date the sender picked
items.body:
`b.mail.agent.expunge` decides whether a message is old enough to destroy from `receivedAt`, and refuses when that is absent. It used to fall back to `internalDate`, which the sender chooses: RFC 9051 section 6.3.12 lets an APPEND carry a date-time, and a backend that records it without stamping its own arrival time produces a row whose only date came from the client. A row dated to the epoch cleared a floor of any size, so an account that can APPEND could date a message into the past and then destroy it inside the window the floor exists to hold.

A missing `receivedAt` is now unknown arrival whatever `internalDate` says, and unknown arrival already refuses. `internalDate` is unchanged for display and for `INTERNALDATE` responses; it is not an input to a destruction decision.

The store that ships stamps both fields with server time, so this was reachable through a backend that honours the APPEND date.

items.title: STARTTLS names the peer it is verifying
items.body:
`b.mail.send` over STARTTLS sets the peer host on the upgraded connection, as the implicit-TLS path already did. Without it, node checks the certificate against `servername || host`, and `servername` is deliberately left undefined for an address literal because an IP is not a valid SNI name. With neither set the check fell back to node's default and verified the peer against `localhost`, so a server presenting a correct IP SAN could not be verified at all.

This was the only client-side upgrade over an existing socket in the framework.

items.title: Every mail listener refuses an option name it does not have
items.body:
`b.mail.server.mx.create`, `.submission.create`, `.imap.create`, `.pop3.create` and `.managesieve.create` throw `mail-server-<name>/bad-opts` naming the unknown key and listing the accepted ones. They accepted anything: a misspelled option left the setting at its default while the caller believed it was set, and afterwards nothing distinguished a typo from an omission. These options decide security posture, so the failure was silent in the direction that matters.

Upgrade note: a call passing a name that was never read now throws where it used to start a listener. That is the point, and the message names the key.

Two names were only ever accepted, never read. `compress` appeared in a source comment describing how to enable COMPRESS=DEFLATE; nothing read it, and the extension is not offered because a compression oracle applies to the encrypted stream. `maxSize` and `depth` are parsed from a GETMETADATA command, not from construction.

items.title: The vendored `@blamejs/pki` bundle moves to 0.6.21
items.body:
`b.mtlsCa` and `b.auth.passkey` are built on the vendored PKI toolkit; `lib/vendor/blamejs-pki.cjs` and its `MANIFEST.json` hashes now carry 0.6.21. The toolkit is internal and is not re-exported, so no blamejs API changes shape.

Two of the fixes in the range harden lookups against a supplied name. A Sigstore bundle whose certificate holds a non-text subjectAltName `otherName` value is no longer read as an identity, so a value whose raw bytes matched a pinned identity can no longer satisfy an identity policy; and an algorithm, curve, digest or profile name that collides with an inherited object property is refused with the verb's own error rather than reaching the lookup. The rest adds CMS composite ML-KEM recipients and the SCEP `getCert`, `getCrl` and CertRep verbs, none of which the framework calls.

The vendored public-suffix list is refreshed to its 2026-09-01 snapshot, which is what `b.cookies` and the origin checks read when deciding registrable domain boundaries.

items.title: `audit` reaches the sink on the listeners that document it
items.body:
`b.mail.server.imap`, `.pop3` and `.managesieve` document an `audit` option and never read it, so an operator who wired a sink received nothing from these three. The sink is now validated at construction, in the same shape every other primitive takes, and receives each event alongside the framework audit rather than in place of it.

Passing `b.audit` itself as that sink names the module the framework trail already writes through, and forwarding to it would append every event twice: two chain rows, and two of whatever an operator alerts on, indistinguishable from a genuine repeat. A sink that is the framework audit is not written a second time. A wrapper around it still is, because the test is identity rather than shape.

items.title: An IMAP literal carries the rest of its own command line
items.body:
The reader consumed a literal's octets and left the CRLF that ends the command line in the buffer, where the next turn read it as a line of its own. An empty command is refused, so a client that completed an APPEND correctly was answered `BAD` after the command had already succeeded.

The bytes after the octets are now read as the rest of that command, whatever the literal's length; a zero-length literal is treated like any other. When nothing follows, the literal was the last argument and reaches the handler as bytes, which is unchanged and is the only way to carry a value that is not text.

A synchronizing literal is answered with a continuation request whatever its length, a zero-byte one included, and the minimum-arrival-rate guard no longer applies to a literal that carries no octets. A client following the specification waits for that `+` before sending the line terminator, so an empty literal that was never answered left both sides waiting.

What follows the octets is what says whether the literal was the last argument, so the reader waits for that line to end rather than deciding from whichever bytes arrived together. RFC 9051 puts the terminator in the command's own grammar, so it is always coming. Deciding on an empty receive buffer would decide on TCP segmentation: `LOGIN {5}` and its octets, split from the arguments that follow, would complete as a whole command with the arguments it had, which for a login is a session authenticated on a fragment. A command now parses the same however it was split.

When something does follow, the literal was not the last token, which RFC 9051 allows wherever an astring is allowed and the `LOGIN` example in section 6.2.3 uses twice on one line. Those bytes continue the command: the body is written back into the line as a quoted string and the line is read again, so a second literal opens the way the first did and a command may carry any number of them.

After a literal's octets the grammar allows the end of the line or a space and more arguments. Anything else is refused, rather than read as this command's arguments, so a client that does not terminate its line cannot have its next command absorbed into the previous one.

A literal's bytes are not charged against the listener's `maxLineBytes`. The wire frames the two separately: that option bounds what arrives as one line, while a literal is framed by its own octet count and bounded by `maxLiteralBytes`, so a short command carrying a large argument is no longer refused as a long line. That holds for a command's later literals as well as its first: each completed one is written back into the line as a quoted string, so by the third the line carried the first two payloads and was refused for their size, on a command whose own syntax is a few dozen bytes. What the literals of one command may add up to is bounded in turn, since a command may carry any number of them, and the last one counts toward that total like the rest. A literal may also be an element of a parenthesized list, where the byte after its octets is the closing paren rather than a space, and that reads as the command it is. A literal that is written back into the command still passes the profile's own command-line cap, which is what bounds how much command text is parsed at all.

A literal that is not the last token is refused when its body cannot be written back as a quoted string: one carrying CR, LF or NUL, or one whose octets are not decodable as UTF-8. A literal carries CHAR8 and need not be text at all, and decoding what is not UTF-8 substitutes a replacement character for each byte it cannot read, which would hand the command a password the client never sent and fail the login as a wrong one. The command is refused, naming the reason, rather than rebuilt into something else. A literal in the last position is never decoded and is unaffected, which is why a password or a search term sent as one still arrives exactly as it was written.

A client that sends a literal's octets and no line terminator now waits, as it does for any unfinished line.

items.title: Tearing a connection down stops the reader that was serving it
items.body:
All five mail listeners close the session, not just the socket. Closing is what marks the session, and that marker is the only thing standing between a torn-down connection and the commands the peer had already queued behind the handler that was running.

`b.mail.server.pop3` and `.managesieve` wire the post-STARTTLS teardown separately from the plaintext one and passed it the upgraded socket alone, so an idle timeout there left the reader believing the session was live: a `DELE` pipelined behind a `STAT` reached the maildrop after the connection was gone.

`b.mail.server.submission` keeps the client's pipelined remainder in its buffer and resumes reading it when a pending command answers. A refused backlog destroyed the socket and left that buffer, so a `MAIL` / `RCPT` / `BDAT ... LAST` queued behind an `AUTH` reached message finalization on a connection the server had already refused.

The bound that refuses such a backlog is also asked where a command starts waiting, not only where bytes arrive. What it measures is how much is held while a verdict is outstanding, and on arrival nothing is outstanding yet: an `AUTH` and an over-cap remainder in one segment were checked before the `AUTH` was taken, so the remainder was never measured.

`b.mail.server.mx` chains each arriving segment behind the previous one and skips the queue once the connection closes, but the flag it reads was written from the socket's own close event. That event arrives a turn later than the queued segment resumes, so a segment that arrived while a gate was still running was processed after the gate tore the connection down.

A session also ends without the listener deciding it, and those paths run no refusal: a peer that pipelines commands behind a slow one and then hangs up, or a socket the server destroys at shutdown. `b.mail.server.imap`, `.managesieve` and `.submission` mark the session on the socket's own close too, so a handler settling afterwards finds the session already over rather than executing what the peer left queued.

The marker is a field of its own rather than a session-stage value, because the stage is the protocol position and handlers assign it: a close landing while a login or a sender check was in flight would otherwise be overwritten when that check answered.

Every POP3 TRANSACTION handler also hands its store call back to the reader. `STAT`, `LIST`, `RETR`, `DELE`, `RSET`, `TOP`, `UIDL` and the UPDATE-state commit registered their work for the session-end wait and returned nothing, so the reader took the next command while the previous one was still in the store.

items.title: A ManageSieve literal is refused rather than repaired when it is not UTF-8
items.body:
`b.mail.server.managesieve` decoded the octets of a `PUTSCRIPT` literal with a conversion that substitutes a replacement character for every byte it cannot read. The substitution happened before anything examined the value, so the script that was validated and stored was a repaired copy: a `0xFF` inside a comment came back as three octets, the stored script was longer than the count the client announced, and the reply was `OK`.

A Sieve script decides what is filed, forwarded and discarded, so a byte altered inside a string, a header name or an address changes what a rule does rather than only how it reads. RFC 5804 section 2.3 requires the script to be verified before it is accepted, and verifying the repaired copy is not verifying what arrived. Such a script is now refused, naming the reason, and nothing reaches the store.

The same conversion ran on an `AUTHENTICATE` initial response sent as a literal. A SASL token is base64, and the replacement character's own bytes fall outside that alphabet, so they are dropped when the token is decoded: two different responses on the wire reached the verifier as one credential. That round is refused too.

items.title: A literal that arrives with its own opener is not pipelined data
items.body:
The listeners bound how much command text may wait while a handler runs. A literal's payload is not waiting: it belongs to the command whose opener announced it, and what bounds it is the literal cap, or for ManageSieve the profile's script cap.

That bound read only the transfer already recorded on the session, and a client that writes an opener and its payload in one segment has not started one yet, so the payload was charged as backlog. `b.mail.server.managesieve` answered `NO` and closed the connection on a `PUTSCRIPT` well inside the profile's script cap, and `b.mail.server.imap` did the same for a literal sent behind a queued command. Whether a script was accepted depended on how the client's write was split.

Both listeners now exempt the declared payload already present in the buffer. What counts as an opener is what the listener's own command parser says opens a literal, so a line that is not a command it has (`BOGUS {1048576+}`) buys no allowance for the bytes behind it. Only one payload is exempt, the first the scan reaches: the reader takes one command at a time, so a second literal pipelined behind the first is waiting, and bytes after the exempt payload are charged as before.

Whether the session is authenticated is not part of that question. A client may pipeline the login and the literal command in one write, and judging the second against the state as it stood before the first refuses a command that is valid by the time the reader reaches it.

That makes the exemption a prediction about a line the reader has not taken. When the reader takes it and refuses the literal, those octets are ordinary queue, so the allowance is applied again per command rather than only when the socket next delivers data, which a single coalesced write never does.

items.title: A command handler must hand its work back to the reader
items.body:
A listener that reads one command at a time is only serialized if its handlers return what they start. A handler that begins asynchronous work as a bare statement returns nothing, the reader has nothing to wait for, and it takes the next command immediately — which is the race the serialization exists to remove, still present on every path except the one that was fixed by hand.

The check refuses that shape in the mail listeners. It names the files that read differently and why: the submission listener holds its buffer on a pending-command flag rather than on a returned promise, and two others read an HTTP request body rather than a command stream.

items.title: Growth measurements share one implementation
items.body:
Eight assertions across five suites timed a scan at two input sizes and divided. Each held its own sample count and its own floor, and at sub-millisecond readings the ratio reports what else the machine was doing: one of them measured 9.5x for 4x input on a shared runner for a scan that measures 3.4x to 4.2x locally.

They now use the shared measurement the framework already had, which declines to take a ratio at all below a floor where a quadratic scan would already have taken seconds, and re-measures with more samples before failing anything.

A ninth was left behind by that sweep, because it measures a protocol round trip and the shared measurement only accepted synchronous work. It kept a single unrepeated reading and failed a run at 9.41 against a bound of 9, on a scan that is linear. The measurement now has an asynchronous form, and a check refuses a ratio taken by hand so the next one cannot be missed by enumeration.

items.title: The mail listeners have live coverage
items.body:
The release gate ran the mail backend's live tests on any change under `lib/mail-server*`, and those tests exercised the SMTP client, DKIM and S/MIME. None of them opened a connection to the IMAP, POP3, ManageSieve or submission listeners, so a change to all five reported a green live run that had not reached them.

A new integration file drives the four listeners over real sockets with certificate verification on, against the shipped mail store on a real database rather than a stand-in, and relays a submitted message onward by SMTP so the delivery assertion is what a receiving server got. It runs whenever a listener changes.

items.title: A `var` read above its own assignment is refused
items.body:
A `var` read before the line that assigns it holds `undefined` rather than raising, so the expression around it yields a value and execution continues with it. A listener option resolved from a profile name assigned eight lines lower took a fallback and bounded literals at the strict number on a permissive listener.

The check refuses a read evaluated in the same scope as the declaration, across `lib/`, `scripts/` and `test/`. A read inside a nested function is left alone: that runs when the function is called, which is after the assignment, and it is the form the codebase uses throughout.

releases.headline: Eleven scans over request data took time proportional to the square of their input
releases.summary:
A pattern with no start anchor retries from every position, so a value made of the one character it is looking for costs time proportional to the SQUARE of its length. Eleven such scans were reachable with request data: an email guard spent 243ms on a 16k value of carriage returns, a JSONPath filter 400ms on a 16k pattern, and an IMAP FETCH, a GPP consent string, a List-Unsubscribe header and an XML entity decoder each about 25ms at the byte cap their own caller enforces. One request, one core, tens of milliseconds each.

All eleven now walk their input once. Behaviour is unchanged: each rewrite was checked against the pattern it replaces over hundreds of thousands of generated inputs.

items.title: Scans over request data run in time proportional to their input
items.body:
Each of these was reachable with a value an attacker chooses, and each cost time proportional to the square of its length:

- `b.guardEmail.sanitize` / `validateMessage`: the smuggled-SMTP-verb scan walked the whitespace after every bare line ending, and a carriage return is itself whitespace, so a value of carriage returns re-walked the same run once per position. 243ms for a single 16k value, now 0.7ms.
- `b.jsonPath`: a `match()` or `search()` filter pattern is translated before it is screened, and the translation restarted at every `[`. A 16k pattern took 400ms, and the pattern carries no length cap. Now 0.9ms.
- `b.iabMspa.parseGpp`: reading the section-ID list off a GPP header cost 25ms at the 8192-character cap.
- `b.mailServer` IMAP: the trailing modifier list on a FETCH cost 25ms at the default 8192-byte line cap.
- `b.mailUnsubscribe`: the `<...>` unwrap on a List-Unsubscribe header, both when validating and when checking the owner address.
- `b.xmlC14n`: the entity decoder, on text inside a signed document.
- `b.aiOutput.sanitize`: the markdown image, link and reference-definition URL extractors, which is the surface the EchoLeak exfiltration gate reads. 218ms for 64 KiB of model output, now 1.4ms.
- `b.forms` numeric bounds, `b.ssrfGuard` hostname normalization, `b.mailStore` full-text tokens, and the trailing-slash trims in `b.acme`, `b.mcp`, `b.queue`, `b.logStream` and the request body parser.

No behaviour changed. Every rewrite was compared against the pattern it replaces across the inputs that reach it, including the case the markdown extractor exists for: an alt text equal to its own target URL, where locating the URL by searching the matched text hits the alt copy and leaves the real target intact.

The scans that walk a run of characters do so without building an index over their input. Two of them first bought linear time with a table of one entry per character, which is the same amplifier aimed at memory: `b.guardEmail` accepts 128 MiB on the permissive profile, so a message that passed the size gate would have allocated 512 MiB beside itself, and a few concurrent ones would exhaust the process. The smuggling scan now carries the whitespace-run boundary in two values during a single backward pass, and the markdown extractors answer their forward-only queries with a position that never moves backwards. Both remain linear in time and now allocate nothing that grows with the input.

The URL extractors report each match to the rewriter as they find it, rather than returning every match together. Model output is accepted up to a `maxBytes` the caller sets, and a response made of many short links produces a match apiece, so holding them all cost a multiple of a response that had already been accepted. Each URL is now spliced as it is found.

items.title: `b.codepointClass` gains three text scans
items.body:
The rewrites above needed the same three operations in several places, so they are primitives rather than a copy per module:

- `trimTrailingChars(text, chars)` removes the run of characters at the end of `text` that are all in `chars`.
- `firstDelimited(text, open, close, from?)` returns the first non-empty `open`...`close` group as `{ body, start, end }`.
- `lastDelimited(text, open, close)` returns the group that ends the text, ignoring trailing whitespace.

Both delimiter scans take single characters and return `null` for anything longer: skipping an empty group advances by one position and searches again, so a longer delimiter would be re-matched from nearly the same place each time. `trimTrailingChars` accepts a set of any size and decides membership once per character in it.

Each walks the text once. The patterns they replace (`/\/+$/`, `/<([^>]+)>/`, `/<([^>]+)>\s*$/`) all restart at every candidate position.

items.title: The vendored `@blamejs/pki` bundle moves to 0.6.14
items.body:
`b.mtlsCa` and `b.auth.passkey` are built on the vendored PKI toolkit; `lib/vendor/blamejs-pki.cjs` and its `MANIFEST.json` hashes now carry 0.6.14. The toolkit is internal and is not re-exported, so no blamejs API changes shape.

The PKCS#12 archives `generateClientP12` writes are unchanged: the classical ECDSA-P384 bridge keeps the RFC 7292 HMAC MacData that pre-3.5 OpenSSL peers can read, the PQC default keeps PBMAC1, and both are authenticated with HMAC-SHA-512. The archive test now reads the digest name alongside the verdict and refuses a wrong password explicitly, so a MAC that verified under SHA-1 would fail the run rather than pass as authenticated.

items.title: A scan may not index its own input
items.body:
A scan over caller-supplied text may no longer build a typed array with one entry per character. Making a scan linear that way spends memory several times the size of the input to save time, and every one of these scans runs under a `maxBytes` the profile sets, so the allocation is a multiple of a limit the operator already chose.

The check reads the shape rather than the intent, so it also covers arrays that are the point rather than a shortcut: `b.guardMarkdown` sizes its bracket index by a delimiter count it refuses above a fixed ceiling, and `b.yaml`'s lexer returns a per-character mask as half of its result. Both are named, with the reason each is not the thing being refused.

items.title: A gate measures what the framework's own patterns cost
items.body:
`b.guardRegex.assertSafe` screens every operator-supplied pattern and `b.regexLinear` runs one without a backtracking engine. Neither had ever been pointed at the patterns the framework itself ships, so a library pattern could run away and nothing would say so.

The new check measures rather than inspects. Screening on shape would refuse ten library patterns that are in fact linear, because a shape that can backtrack usually does not; what separates the ones worth fixing is that a single call cost tens of milliseconds at the byte cap its caller enforces. So the gate asks for both: expensive at 8192 characters, and still growing faster than its input between 8k and 32k. It reads every regex literal in the library, not the ones written in a particular place, after a first version that only read `var X = /re/;` declarations walked straight past a pattern written inline.

A pattern that can backtrack is measured in a separate process under a deadline, so a pattern whose cost doubles with every character added is named and reported rather than hanging the run. What separates that from a probe that merely ran out of time is how long the match interrupted at the deadline had been running: one match still going after five seconds is the runaway, while many short matches that each returned are just a slow machine. In the second case the probe resumes in a fresh process from the subject it was on, carrying its worst measurement forward. A pattern that never finishes its measurement is reported too, since a pattern the gate could not measure is not one it has cleared.

releases.headline: Every framework error code is namespace/code, and an empty CSP is refused rather than emitted
releases.summary:
An error code is the thing operators branch on, and the framework spelled it three ways. Most codes were `namespace/kebab-case`, 28 guards used a dot instead of a slash, and roughly 970 codes across 83 modules were bare `UPPER_SNAKE` with no namespace at all: `catch (e) { e.code === "BAD_OPT" }` matched a cache error, a queue error and a signing error alike, and told you nothing about which subsystem refused. Every framework error code is now `namespace/code`.

`b.csp.build` returned an empty string for a directive set that emitted nothing, which sets a Content-Security-Policy header that constrains nothing while reading, at the call site, as a policy that was set. It refuses now, the way the sibling `b.cdnCacheControl.build` already refused an empty Cache-Control list.

items.title: An empty Content-Security-Policy is refused instead of emitted
items.body:
`b.csp.build` returned `""` when the directive set produced nothing to emit. Assigned to a header, that is a CSP that constrains nothing, and at the call site it reads as a policy that was configured. A directive set assembled conditionally, where every branch happened to be skipped, produced exactly that.

Three inputs reached it: an empty object, an array (`typeof [] === "object"` passes an object check and `Object.keys([])` is empty), and a set whose every directive carries an empty value list. All three are now refused with `csp/empty`. A non-empty array was already refused, since its index `"0"` is not a directive name.

The refusal lives where emptiness is decided, so it covers `build` and `mergeDirectives` alike. A merge that adds nothing to a non-empty base is still a no-op and still returns the base policy.

items.title: Error codes are `namespace/code` everywhere
items.body:
**This changes error codes you may be matching on.** Every framework error now carries a namespaced, kebab-case code:

- `BAD_OPT` from `b.cache` is now `cache/bad-opt`; from `b.queue`, `queue/bad-opt`
- `NOT_FOUND` from an object-store backend is now `objectstore/not-found`
- `html.bad-profile` is now `html/bad-profile`, and the same for archive, csv, cidr, domain, email, filename, graphql, image, json, jsonpath, jwt, markdown, mime, oauth, pdf, regex, shell, sql, svg, text, xml, yaml and the rest of the guard family
- `auditDailyReview/...`, a camelCase namespace, is now `audit-daily-review/...`
- `b.httpClient` spelled its own namespace two ways; every code is now `http-client/...`
- `NOT_LEADER`, raised by every write-side gate on a follower, is now `cluster/not-leader`
- `b.mailBounce.parse` raised `missing-vendor` and `unknown-vendor` with no namespace at all; both now carry `mail-bounce/`

The same name previously meant different things in different modules, so a caller could not tell a cache refusal from a queue refusal without reading the message. Matching on the namespaced code is exact, and `e.code.split("/")[0]` gives the subsystem.

**Rule ids are unchanged and stay dotted.** `filename.traversal`, `archive.absolute-path` and their siblings identify which rule fired on a piece of content, and a content refusal still carries that id as its error code. The separator is what tells the two apart: a dot names a rule, a slash names a framework error.

**Codes that mirror an external vocabulary keep their spelling.** A timeout raised as `ETIMEDOUT` stays `ETIMEDOUT` so a generic errno classifier still recognizes it, and `CIRCUIT_OPEN` is held un-namespaced through the pre-1.0 line as previously documented.

Refusals raised by the shared option validators now name the check that failed rather than a generic code: an option that must be an object reports `validate-opts/bad-object`, an unknown option `validate-opts/unknown-opt`, and a negative value where a non-negative one was required `validate-opts/bad-non-negative-finite`.

items.title: `sandbox` with no value emits the directive instead of nothing
items.body:
`b.csp.build({ sandbox: [] })` returned an empty string. A `sandbox` directive with no value applies every sandbox restriction, so that is the strictest policy the builder can express, and it was the one input that produced a header constraining nothing.

It now emits `sandbox`. `sandbox` with values is unchanged, and the two other valueless directives (`upgrade-insecure-requests`, `block-all-mixed-content`) already behaved this way.

items.title: An option refusal reported a different code depending on the error class
items.body:
The shared option validators resolve the code two ways: through the error class's factory when it has one, and through its constructor otherwise. Only the constructor path read the default code the calling module named, so the same failure surfaced as a bare `BAD_OPT` against a class with a factory and as the module's own code against a class without one.

Both paths now resolve the code the same way, which means a validator refusal carries the code its caller specified. `b.vc.verifyPresentation` with a missing credential-options object, for one, reported `BAD_OPT` and now reports `validate-opts/bad-object`.

items.title: The error-code check reads every construction the framework uses
items.body:
The in-repo check that holds error codes to `namespace/kebab-case` inspected `new SomeError("...")` and `SomeError.factory("...")`. It never inspected the `_err("...")` alias that seventy library files call, the code passed to a shared validator after the error class, a code set as a plain property, or a module's own error helper under a local name. Each of those carried codes the check could not see, which is how three spellings coexisted without anything going red.

It now reads all of them, and it finds a module's error helper by looking at what the function does rather than matching a list of expected names.

releases.headline: The audit purge anchor is signed — three statements could erase an audit trail and leave the chain verifying clean
releases.summary:
The purge anchor is the one thing in the audit chain that says rows are ALLOWED to be missing. Every other tamper check compares a stored hash against a recomputed one, so deleting rows leaves a gap that verification catches; the anchor closes that gap by declaration. It was accepted on shape alone — 128 hex characters and a whole number — which is exactly what an attacker with write access supplies. Delete the rows, delete the checkpoints covering them, insert an anchor naming any hash and counter, and `b.audit.verify` reported a clean chain. That is fewer steps than the relink-and-forge attack the chain already refuses, and it erases more.

The anchor now carries a post-quantum signature over every field a reader acts on, and every place that reads it verifies it first: the chain walk, the contiguity guard on the next purge, the predecessor lookup that grounds the next archive's proof, and the append path itself, which needs the boundary to know where a purged chain resumes.

Upgrading with an existing purge anchor requires one boot with `acceptUnsignedPurgeAnchor: true`; see Migration.

items.title: A purge anchor must prove it was written with the audit-signing key (#674)
items.body:
`b.auditChain.verifyChain` adopted `lastPurgedRowHash` as the chain origin and skipped every row at or below `lastPurgedCounter` after checking only that the hash was 128 hex characters and the counter was a whole number. Both are trivially satisfiable by anyone who can write to the database, and the result was a verification that reported success over an arbitrary quantity of deleted history.

The anchor now carries `signature` and `publicKeyFingerprint`, signed by `b.auditSign` over the scope, boundary counter, boundary row hash, archive identifier and purge time. The signed layout is newline-delimited and refuses a newline inside any string field at both sign and verify time, so one signature can never verify two different readings of the same bytes. A boundary counter beyond `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` is refused for the same reason: the column is a BIGINT and the signed bytes carry the counter as text, so above that range two distinct stored values render identically and one signature would cover both. The same bound now applies wherever a counter is rendered into bytes that get signed — the consumer chain anchors in `b.auditSign` and the origin a `b.chainWriter` resumes from — through one shared predicate rather than three spellings of it. Its format string is distinct from the checkpoint and consumer-anchor formats, so a signature minted for one can never be replayed as another.

`b.auditChain.verifyPurgeAnchor` reports a status rather than a boolean, because the ways an anchor can fail to verify call for different reactions: `unsigned`, `forged`, `corrupt`, and `unchecked` — the last meaning the process holds no signing key and could not perform the check at all. Collapsing `unchecked` into `forged` would raise a tamper alarm on a healthy volume every time an offline verifier ran, and collapsing it into success would accept anything.

A clean result over a purge now says what was established and what was not: the boundary counter, whether the signature verified, the archive the anchor names, and whether anything actually found it. A signature proves this framework wrote the boundary; it says nothing about whether the archive still exists or holds those rows, and a report that ran the two together would be the wrong thing to hand an auditor.

Only the consumer knows where bundles are kept, so the check is theirs to supply: `b.auditChain.verifyChain(..., { resolveArchive })`, `b.db.init({ resolvePurgeArchive })` for the boot verify, and `blamejs audit verify-chain --archive-dir` for an offline one. With it, a boundary whose archive cannot be produced fails the verify instead of licensing the gap. Both resolvers are refused at the point they are supplied when they are present but not callable: they are consulted only when callable, so a typo or a config that failed to load would remove the very check that was asked for and return a clean result — a gap nothing can ever show the contents of. Without it the walk proceeds and the result says the archive was not resolved.

items.title: The next purge verifies the anchor it is about to extend
items.body:
Checking the anchor only at read time would have left it forgeable through the writer. An unsigned anchor carrying the real predecessor hash, followed by a legitimate purge of the next archive, would have had that purge sign the enlarged boundary — laundering the earlier deletion permanently, under a valid signature.

`b.auditTools.purge` verifies the existing anchor before extending it, and `b.auditTools.exportSlice` verifies it before using its hash to ground the next archive's chain proof. The signature is also computed before the rows are deleted rather than after: signing afterwards means an unavailable key leaves the rows already gone and an unsigned anchor over an unrecoverable deletion, which is the state a reader is now required to refuse. Failing before the delete costs nothing — the archive is on disk and the purge can be re-run.

items.title: A purge is a single-writer operation, start to finish
items.body:
Reading the anchor, deciding the new boundary is contiguous with it, and writing that boundary are one decision. Split across two steps they were two, and two overlapping purges could each find themselves contiguous with the same anchor and each overwrite the other's boundary — leaving rows deleted with nothing accounting for them, which verification then reports as clean, because the anchor is what licenses absence.

The whole sequence now runs under the audit chain's append lock, so an append cannot land between the deletion and the anchor that explains it either. `b.auditTools.purge` and `b.auditTools.signExistingPurgeAnchor` additionally require cluster leadership, which is what appends already require.

Leadership is not enough on its own, so the anchor also carries a fencing token. A superseded leader still holds a working handle, and during a handoff two nodes can both believe they hold it — no agreement between processes can settle that, only what is already stored. A purge reads the token before deleting anything and refuses outright if it has been passed, and the anchor write is refused by the database on the same test.

The boundary itself is fenced too, and separately from the token, because a boundary may only ever advance. A leader holding a HIGHER token can still be proposing a smaller range legitimately, and allowing that while another node was midway through deleting a larger one would leave rows above the surviving boundary gone with nothing accounting for them — the one state the anchor exists to make impossible. Held by the database, so no ordering between the two nodes has to be reasoned about.

`b.clusterStorage.fencedUpsert` is that operation, shared with the audit tip, which had the only implementation of it: MySQL can neither express the condition nor report the refusal, so it needs a read-back the other dialects do not, and one copy of that is enough.

items.title: A cluster purge can actually delete the rows it archived
items.body:
`b.frameworkSchema.ensureSchema` installs an append-only BEFORE-DELETE trigger on `audit_log` and `audit_checkpoints` for every dialect — that trigger is why a privileged actor cannot quietly remove an audit row. The cluster branch of the purge deleted straight through it, on the stated assumption that external databases had no such triggers, so a purge against Postgres or MySQL was refused by the guard every time.

With the boundary now recorded before the deletion, that refusal would leave the anchor advanced over rows still present, which verification then skips.

On Postgres the guard is never taken off and never switched off. It decides per row, permitting a DELETE only for a row at or below the boundary the purge anchor records — and the anchor is written before the rows go, so the guard allows exactly what the purge will remove and refuses everything else. Nothing is granted, which matters: a session setting is not an authorization, because `SET LOCAL` is available to any session holding the framework's own role, so a guard that honoured one could be self-granted by exactly the caller it exists to stop. What the guard does not do is worth stating, because the shape invites the opposite assumption: it does not stop a role that can UPDATE the anchor table, which can raise the boundary, delete what widening permits, and restore the signed row before committing. No rule expressible in a trigger closes that, because the same role supplies the input the rule reads. Making it authoritative against the application's own role needs an authorization that role cannot assume — a separate database role owning these tables and granting no UPDATE on the anchor, or append-only storage underneath — which is a deployment decision the schema cannot make for you. The guard covers the rest: an accidental DELETE from application code, and any role holding DML on the audit tables but not on the anchor. The detection that does not depend on privileges is the chain itself, where removing rows above the boundary breaks the hash linkage and removing the newest ones is what the tip sidecar's rollback check catches. **Installing the guard on MySQL needs a privilege worth checking before you upgrade.** With binary logging enabled — the default — MySQL refuses `CREATE TRIGGER` from a role without `SUPER`, and the `TRIGGER` privilege alone is not sufficient (measured on 8.4, where adding `SET_ANY_DEFINER` does not help either). Grant `SUPER` to the role the framework connects as, or set `log_bin_trust_function_creators=1` on the server. Boot now fails with an error naming both, instead of passing MySQL's own message through — a message that mentions neither the audit guard being installed nor the privilege that is missing. It is a failure rather than a warning on purpose: a volume reported as append-only with no guard on it is the worse outcome. MySQL and SQLite carry the same rule, so no dialect drops its guard for a purge any more. MySQL expresses the condition with `IF … THEN SIGNAL …; END IF`; the semicolon inside makes the body compound, which a protocol driver sends as one message — `DELIMITER` is a command-line construct, and the guard had been shaped around a test harness that needed it. SQLite carries the condition in a `WHEN` clause. Both, and Postgres, wrap the comparison in `COALESCE(..., FALSE)`: with no anchor row the comparison is NULL, and a guard that read that as no-restriction would leave the volume that has never authorized a deletion the least protected one.

That closes a window the previous approach left open — while a purge ran, any other connection holding the framework role could delete audit rows too, and a process killed mid-purge left the guard off until the next boot. The guard now stays installed throughout, on every dialect, including `consent_log`'s and every UPDATE guard, which no purge has any reason to touch.

Behind that trigger sat a second defect the deletion had never reached: it built its SQL without the active dialect, so on MySQL the boundary column was double-quoted and read as a string literal — the comparison failed with a truncated-value error rather than deleting anything. Both are fixed, and a cluster purge is now exercised end to end against live Postgres and MySQL rather than through an injected no-op.

items.title: An interrupted purge can be finished by re-running it
items.body:
The boundary is recorded before the rows it covers are deleted, because the two writes cannot be one transaction and the other order fails worse: a fence refused after the deletion would leave rows gone with nothing accounting for them, which no later purge can repair. Recording first means a refusal deletes nothing.

If the deletion then fails, the boundary describes rows that are still present, and verification skips them. Re-running the same archive now completes that deletion instead of being turned away as non-contiguous — read literally it is non-contiguous, and refusing it would have made the only repair available the one thing the guard rejected. Replaying an archive whose range the anchor already names deletes rows that are already gone, so nothing is gained by replaying one either.

"The same archive" means the whole range, not just where it ended. The anchor records `firstPurgedCounter` alongside the boundary and signs it, so an archive that ends at the same counter but starts later is a different, smaller archive and is refused. Without that, such a bundle would have passed as a retry, deleted everything through the boundary, and left the rows before its own start with no retained copy anywhere.

An anchor written before that field was covered still verifies: when the stored range start is `0` — the only value such an anchor can hold, and one that means the same thing in both layouts — verification retries against the shorter signed bytes. Such an anchor is held to the boundary alone when a retry is judged, too: chain counters begin at 1, so a stored `0` records no start rather than claiming one, and requiring it to equal the archive's start would turn away the very bundle that could finish an interrupted purge there — the contiguity check refuses it as well, since the anchor already ends where that archive ends. An anchor claiming a non-zero start gets no second chance, so this cannot be used to drop the field from an anchor that has one, and producing either signature still requires the signing key.

items.title: An audit write stops when the anchor cannot be believed
items.body:
Boot has always refused to start on an audit chain it cannot verify. The same now applies to tampering that happens while the process is running: if the purge anchor is present and does not verify, `b.audit.record` throws `audit/purge-anchor-not-verified` rather than starting a fresh chain.

Starting over looks like the cautious choice and is the opposite. The new rows would link to `ZERO_HASH` and, on a table a purge had emptied, take counters at or below the boundary the anchor claims — the range `verifyChain` skips. Every write between the tampering and the next verification would land there, linked to nothing and invisible to the check meant to catch it. Refusing costs an audit row; the alternative costs the chain its meaning.

items.title: A chain that resumes after a purge keeps its counters
items.body:
`b.audit.record` derived the next `monotonicCounter` from `MAX(monotonicCounter)`, which an emptied table answers with nothing. After a purge that removed every row, the next process restart therefore restarted the counter at 1 — at or below the purge boundary, which is exactly the range `verifyChain` skips. The rows were written, linked correctly to each other, and excluded from every verification that ever ran over them, with nothing reporting it.

The counter now resumes above the recorded boundary, alongside the hash. Both come from the same verified anchor, read once and cached, so neither can be restored without the other. In a cluster that cache also expires when leadership moves: a purge runs on one node, and a node that led before it and leads again after it would otherwise still hold the pre-purge answer and link its next row to nothing — turning a legitimate purge into a reported chain break. The fencing token is what crosses nodes, so an origin read under an earlier term is re-read rather than trusted. The read itself is a database round trip, so the term is checked again once it returns: an origin fetched just before another node purged describes a chain that no longer exists, and noticing on the next append would be too late for the row this one is about to write. Leadership that will not settle refuses the append instead of linking to a boundary that may already be superseded and an append does not pay for a database read per row.

A purge discards that cached answer before it releases the chain lock. A counter primed while the purge was midway through — after the rows were deleted, before the anchor accounting for them was written — would otherwise have survived as 1 for the life of the process.

items.title: A mail TLS pair that will not load says which file is wrong (#672)
items.body:
`b.mail.server.tls.context` refused a bad certificate pair with OpenSSL's own text and named neither file — `error:05800074:x509 certificate routines::key values mismatch` and nothing else. Those are the two commonest operator mistakes with a TLS pair, both arrive at boot with the server refusing to start, and in both cases the next question is which file: a host mid-renewal has several candidates and usually a symlink, and this function is the only thing that knows which pair it just compared.

The refusal now leads with what is wrong in words, lists the certificate and key paths, and keeps the OpenSSL string after them rather than instead of them. Paths only — a key supplied as a vault-sealed blob is named by its path, never by anything it unsealed to.

**An empty or truncated file is now refused at startup instead of accepted.** This came out of testing the above and is the more serious half. `createSecureContext` does not object to a missing certificate — a context without one is what a TLS *client* uses, and is perfectly legal — so a mail server handed an empty `certFile` started cleanly, advertised STARTTLS, and failed every handshake at runtime. An interrupted renewal leaves exactly that file, and the failure surfaced as far as it is possible to get from its cause. A file holding no PEM block is refused by name.

Where the framework knows which file is at fault it names that one; naming both is reserved for the mismatch, where each file is individually fine and only the pair is wrong.

items.title: A failed open no longer leaves the decrypted database behind (#678)
items.body:
Under `atRest: "encrypted"` the live database is a decrypted working copy in `tmpDir`, and `removePlaintextFiles()` is what stops it outliving the process that made it. An open that threw AFTER claiming that copy never reached it: `close()` returned immediately when `initialized` was false, and that flag says only that init did not FINISH — nothing about what it had already taken. So a failed open left plaintext exactly where the design says none persists, in the case nobody is watching, because the caller saw a throw and moved on.

The claim is now tracked in its own right. `close()` releases it, and `b.db.init` releases it itself when it throws, so recovery does not depend on the caller remembering a `close()` in a `catch`. It is deliberately NOT keyed on the working-copy path alone: that path survives a previous open in the same process, and cleaning up on it would delete a different database's copy when an open failed before claiming anything.

Removing the files also closes the database handle first. Windows refuses to unlink a file another handle holds open, and those unlinks swallow their errors — so on a path that never closed the handle, the ownership record beside the copy disappeared while the decrypted database stayed, which in a directory listing reads exactly like a cleanup that worked.

The stale sweep can also see what it leaves. It enumerated names ending in `.db`, and the ownership record is `<name>.db.owner` — so a record whose working copy was gone was invisible to it permanently, one more every time an open failed, in the directory that holds decrypted databases. It now enumerates on the prefix and considers both names as one volume. A record whose owner is still running is left alone, because the claim is written BEFORE the copy exists and that is what a peer mid-open looks like; one whose owner is gone, or that is too damaged to name an owner at all, is reclaimed. That last case is a deliberate departure from the rule governing an actual database, where anything unprovable is left alone: removing a database costs data, while a record accounting for nothing costs only the pile it builds.

A refusal that arrives once the handle is live is the one case where the copy is deliberately kept: if the final re-encryption also fails, removing it would discard migrations and schema work that committed before the verifications ran, while leaving the older encrypted volume in place — so the next boot would re-run migration steps it holds no record of applying. The copy stays, the failed re-encryption is logged, and the ownership record beside it lets a later boot reclaim or adopt it once this process is gone.

items.title: A read-only open no longer tries to migrate the volume it is inspecting
items.body:
`b.db.init({ readOnly: true })` ran the declarative schema reconcile like any other open. That is a no-op only when the live schema already matches the declaration — and a volume written by an earlier version does not match, because it is missing whatever columns that version had not declared yet. Reconcile answered the difference with `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN`, the handle refused the write, and the open failed.

So the flag whose purpose is inspecting a database without touching it worked on every volume except the older ones an inspection is most likely to be about — and this release, which adds two columns to the purge-anchor table, would have made that the common case.
